chronic-kidney-disease.scope: CKD progression, anemia of CKD (erythropoietin deficiency), mineral and bone disorder, uremic complications, volume overload, indications for emergent dialysis (AEIOU), vascular access
chronic-kidney-disease.core: Persistent kidney injury or reduced filtration causes progressive cardiovascular, metabolic and uremic complications; dialysis follows clinical indications rather than creatinine alone.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Diabetes, hypertension, glomerular disease, obstruction, recurrent AKI, inherited cystic disease
NSAIDs, smoking and uncontrolled proteinuria accelerate progression

rows.label: Clues
items: Early disease often asymptomatic; advanced disease → fatigue, pruritus, anorexia, edema
Uremia: confusion, myoclonus, pericardial friction rub, nausea or bleeding despite normal platelet count
Labs: normocytic anemia, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, ↑phosphate, low/normal calcium

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Nephron loss → hyperfiltration in remaining nephrons, proteinuria and fibrosis
↓Erythropoietin → anemia; phosphate retention/↓calcitriol → ↓calcium absorption → four-gland secondary hyperparathyroidism
Renal bone disease: ↓calcitriol → **deficient osteoid mineralization**, atraumatic fracture; ↑PTH → subperiosteal resorption

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **eGFR <60** or kidney-damage markers for **≥3 months** establishes CKD
Urine albumin/creatinine ratio, urinalysis, creatinine trend; ultrasound for size/obstruction
Stage by GFR and albuminuria; small echogenic kidneys support chronicity but are not universal
Monitor CBC, ferritin/TSAT, K, bicarbonate, calcium, phosphate and PTH

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Albuminuric CKD → **ACE inhibitor/ARB**; monitor creatinine/K; never combine both
SGLT2 inhibitor for T2DM or qualifying albuminuric CKD/HF, generally starting eGFR ≥20
Overload → salt restriction, furosemide; high phosphate → phosphorus restriction, sevelamer; severe hyperparathyroidism → calcitriol
Iron repletion before ESA for selected persistent anemia; correct clinically significant metabolic acidosis
★ **Dialysis (AEIOU)**: refractory acidosis/hyperkalemia/overload (anuria: no diuretics), dialyzable toxins, uremic complications

rows.label: Complications
items: Cardiovascular death, fractures, severe hyperkalemic arrhythmia, malnutrition
Dialysis access infection/thrombosis; rapid urea reduction → dialysis disequilibrium
Peritoneal dialysis + fever/abdominal pain → first **peritoneal fluid cell count, Gram stain, culture**

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Preserve arm veins; plan **AV fistula** before hemodialysis; temporary catheter for emergencies; early transplant referral
BP/glycemic control, avoid nephrotoxins, renal drug adjustment; hepatitis B vaccination before dialysis

rows.label: Mimics
items: AKI: acute creatinine change; may complicate established CKD
Prerenal azotemia: reversible perfusion deficit without persistent structural injury

chronic-lymphocytic-leukemia.name: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia
chronic-lymphocytic-leukemia.scope: Asymptomatic lymphocytosis, smudge cells, flow cytometry (CD5/CD19/CD20/CD23), Rai/Binet staging, hypogammaglobulinemia, autoimmune hemolytic anemia, Richter transformation
chronic-lymphocytic-leukemia.core: An older adult with persistent clonal mature B-cell lymphocytosis may have indolent CLL requiring observation rather than immediate treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older age, male sex, family history; frequently discovered incidentally on CBC

rows.label: Clues
items: Painless lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly; smear with small mature lymphocytes and **smudge cells**
Recurrent sinopulmonary infection suggests hypogammaglobulinemia
★ Rapid asymmetric node growth, fever, weight loss and ↑LDH → **Richter transformation**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Accumulation of dysfunctional clonal B lymphocytes in blood, marrow and lymphoid tissue
Immune dysregulation causes antibody deficiency and autoimmune cytopenias

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Flow cytometry**: clonal B cells coexpress **CD5/CD19/CD23**, weak CD20 and surface immunoglobulin
Clonal B-cell count **≥5000/µL for ≥3 months** supports CLL; lower count without disease → MBL
Smudge cells alone not diagnostic; nodal disease with lower circulating count → SLL
CBC, examination, hemolysis studies/DAT for anemia; marrow biopsy not routinely needed for diagnosis
Before treatment: assess TP53/del(17p), IGHV and TLS risk; suspected transformation → node biopsy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Asymptomatic early disease → **watchful waiting** with clinical/CBC follow-up
Progressive marrow failure, bulky symptomatic disease, B symptoms or refractory autoimmune cytopenias → treatment
**Acalabrutinib/zanubrutinib** or venetoclax + obinutuzumab; regimen chosen by genetics/comorbidity
Autoimmune hemolytic anemia → glucocorticoids; severe recurrent infections with low IgG → selected IVIG
Venetoclax → gradual escalation with tumor-lysis prevention and monitoring

rows.label: Complications
items: Bacterial infections, warm autoimmune hemolysis, immune thrombocytopenia, second cancers
BTK inhibitors → bleeding/atrial arrhythmia; anti-CD20 drugs → HBV reactivation

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Vaccinate before immunosuppression; avoid live vaccines during significant immunocompromise
Screen HBV before anti-CD20 treatment; skin surveillance and routine cancer screening

rows.label: Mimics
items: Reactive lymphocytosis: transient, polyclonal cells
Mantle cell lymphoma: CD5-positive but usually CD23-negative, cyclin D1-positive

colorectal-cancer-screening.name: Colorectal cancer screening
colorectal-cancer-screening.scope: Average-risk screening age 45-75, colonoscopy, FIT, high-risk screening (family history, Lynch syndrome, IBD), post-polypectomy surveillance
colorectal-cancer-screening.core: Screen average-risk adults ages 45–75; every positive noncolonoscopy screening test requires diagnostic colonoscopy.

rows.label: Who
items: Average risk: no CRC/adenoma history, IBD or hereditary syndrome; FDR = first-degree relative
★ Symptoms or iron deficiency anemia → **diagnostic evaluation**, regardless of screening age
FDR CRC/advanced polyp <60 or ≥2 affected FDRs → high-risk family pathway

rows.label: Start/stop
items: Ages 76–85: individualize by health, preference and prior screening; stop after 85
★ High-risk family → start **40 or 10 years before youngest diagnosis**, whichever earlier
Family-risk colonoscopy every 5 years; one FDR ≥60 → start 40, routine intervals

rows.label: Test
items: ★ **Colonoscopy every 10 years** or **FIT annually** are common strategies
Stool DNA–FIT every 1–3 years; CT colonography every 5 years
Flexible sigmoidoscopy every 5 years, or every 10 years plus annual FIT

rows.label: IF positive
items: Positive FIT/stool DNA/CT study → colonoscopy; repeating stool test cannot clear the result
Post-polypectomy intervals assume complete removal, adequate preparation and high-quality examination

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ Lynch: colonoscopy roughly age 20–25 every 1–2 years; gene/family history can modify
Colonic IBD: surveillance about 8 years after onset; PSC → begin at diagnosis
Routine stool testing between scheduled high-quality surveillance colonoscopies adds little benefit

congenital-heart-disease.name: Congenital heart disease
congenital-heart-disease.scope: Cyanotic heart disease (5 Ts: Tetralogy of Fallot, TGA, truncus, tricuspid atresia, TAPVR), acyanotic heart disease (VSD, ASD, PDA, coarctation of aorta), hyperoxia test, prostaglandin E1
congenital-heart-disease.core: Neonatal cyanosis or shock as the ductus closes demands urgent assessment for duct-dependent congenital heart disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Maternal diabetes, congenital rubella, family history; Down syndrome → AV septal defects
Prematurity → PDA; Turner syndrome → coarctation

rows.label: Clues
items: Poor feeding, diaphoresis, tachypnea, hepatomegaly → infant heart failure
VSD: harsh holosystolic lower-left sternal murmur; ASD: **fixed split S2**, pulmonic flow murmur, RV volume overload
PDA: continuous machinery murmur, bounding pulses; coarctation: weak femoral pulses, arm–leg BP gradient
Central cyanosis: blue lips/tongue, warm extremities → **low arterial saturation**; peripheral: cold extremities

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Left-to-right shunts (VSD, ASD, extracardiac PDA) increase pulmonary flow; remodeling can reverse flow → Eisenmenger syndrome
Duct-dependent lesions require pulmonary/systemic flow or mixing through fetal communications
High neonatal PVR limits VSD shunt → murmur appears/louder over weeks as **PVR falls**

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Preductal/right-hand and postductal/foot oxygen saturation; **echocardiography** defines anatomy
★ Hyperoxia test: little PaO2 rise with 100% oxygen suggests cardiac shunting; echo preferred
ECG and chest radiograph support diagnosis; normal murmur does not exclude critical disease

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected duct-dependent lesion → **prostaglandin E1** immediately; monitor for apnea
★ Tet spell (agitation, softer murmur) → knee–chest, oxygen, fluids, morphine; refractory → phenylephrine or propranolol
TGA with inadequate mixing → balloon atrial septostomy, then arterial switch
Large shunts → diuretics, closure; premature PDA → ibuprofen; **obstructed TAPVR → emergency repair**
Coarctation → repair; post-repair paradoxical hypertension → **IV beta-blocker**; Eisenmenger → **do not close shunt**

rows.label: Complications
items: Pulmonary hypertension, failure to thrive, arrhythmias, infective endocarditis
Right-to-left shunting → brain abscess, paradoxical emboli, secondary erythrocytosis

rows.label: Prevention
items: Pulse-ox newborn screening; rubella immunization before pregnancy; maternal glycemic control
Endocarditis prophylaxis for selected unrepaired cyanotic or prosthetic-material lesions during dental procedures

rows.label: Mimics
items: Lung disease: substantial oxygen response, pulmonary findings
PPHN: elevated pulmonary resistance with structurally normal heart

table.title: Five cyanotic lesions
rows: RV obstruction, VSD, overriding aorta, RVH; boot-shaped heart
Parallel circuits; single S2; egg-on-string silhouette
Pulmonary veins drain systemically; obstruction → edema

congenital-heart-disease.evidence: Not checked online; established pediatric cardiology teaching.

contraception.name: Contraception
contraception.scope: Combined oral contraceptives, progestin-only pills, implant, intrauterine devices, tubal sterilization
contraception.core: Choose contraception through shared decisions about efficacy, bleeding, reversibility, adherence, and estrogen-related vascular risk.

rows.label: Who
items: Anyone seeking pregnancy prevention; adolescents and nulliparous patients can use IUDs or implants
Healthy patient: blood pressure suffices; **no pelvic exam** needed before oral contraceptives

rows.label: Schedule
items: Pills daily; depot medroxyprogesterone every 3 months; implants/IUDs last years (product-dependent)
★ Emergency contraception ≤**5 days**: copper IUD/ulipristal; levonorgestrel ≤72 h, no medical contraindications
Progestin-only pills: daily timing crucial; norethindrone less forgiving than drospirenone

rows.label: Special groups
items: Breastfeeding (estrogen lowers milk volume, protein) or estrogen contraindication → progestin-only or copper IUD
Current breast cancer → copper IUD; avoid hormonal methods
Prior VTE, poor adherence → **IUD/implant** (depot raises VTE risk); older exams: depot, avoid IUD after STI

rows.label: Choice
items: Combined pills: suppress ovulation, improve acne/cramps, reduce endometrial/ovarian cancer risk
★ **LARC** minimizes adherence failures; condoms add STI protection
Tubal sterilization: permanent; counsel regret, alternatives, surgical risk, ectopic risk after failure

rows.label: Contraindications
items: ★ Estrogen: **migraine with aura, prior VTE/thrombophilia**, hypertension (stop pill), early postpartum
Smoking age ≥35: combined methods usually avoid; ≥15 cigarettes/day → absolute contraindication
IUD: pregnancy, cervicitis/PID, distorted cavity (non-distorting fibroid OK); copper: also Wilson disease

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ Same-day STI screening need not delay insertion without cervicitis; prior PID alone permits IUD
Sterilization: voluntary informed consent; no required partner approval, parity, or marital status
After ulipristal, wait 5 days before progestin; backup contraception needed after hormonal restart

table.title: Long-acting choices
rows: Treats heavy menses; atrophy → expected benign amenorrhea

copd.name: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
copd.scope: Stable COPD, acute exacerbation (AECOPD), oxygen-induced hypercapnia, noninvasive ventilation (NIV/BiPAP), indications for intubation, bronchodilators and glucocorticoids
copd.core: Persistent airflow obstruction after inhalational exposure causes progressive exertional dyspnea and episodic infectious or inflammatory exacerbations.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Tobacco, biomass smoke, occupational dusts; alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency with early/basilar emphysema

rows.label: Clues
items: Chronic cough/sputum, prolonged expiration, wheeze, hyperinflation
★ **Somnolence, exhaustion, silent chest, worsening acidosis** → impending respiratory failure
Exacerbation: ↑dyspnea, purulent sputum, rhonchi, **no infiltrate** → acute bronchitis, not pneumonia

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Small-airway inflammation + alveolar destruction → expiratory collapse, air trapping, impaired diffusion
Excess oxygen worsens CO₂ retention mainly through V/Q mismatch and Haldane effect

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Postbronchodilator FEV₁/FVC <0.70** confirms persistent obstruction in compatible clinical setting
Exacerbation: pulse oximetry; ABG for severe distress/altered mentation; radiograph for pneumonia, edema, pneumothorax
Consider ECG, troponin, BNP, or PE evaluation when symptoms exceed expected exacerbation pattern

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Exacerbation → **albuterol + ipratropium**, prednisone for 5 days; titrate oxygen to 88–92%
Antibiotics: purulence + increased dyspnea/sputum volume, or ventilatory support; doxycycline/azithromycin options
★ Hypercapnic acidosis, pH ≤7.35 → **BiPAP** unless aspiration risk, arrest, instability, inability to cooperate
Intubate for failed NIV, severe encephalopathy, refractory hypoxemia, or inability to protect airway
Long-term oxygen if stable PaO₂ ≤55 or saturation ≤88%; selected cor pulmonale/polycythemia with PaO₂ 56–59

rows.label: Complications
items: Pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale, secondary polycythemia, cachexia
Pneumonia risk with inhaled steroids; ventilation → dynamic hyperinflation, auto-PEEP, barotrauma

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Smoking cessation**, influenza/COVID/pneumococcal/RSV vaccination when eligible, pulmonary rehabilitation
Check inhaler technique/adherence; offer alpha-1 antitrypsin testing at least once

rows.label: Mimics
items: Asthma: variable symptoms and reversible obstruction
Heart failure: orthopnea, edema, vascular congestion; bronchiectasis: copious sputum, dilated bronchi

table.title: Stable inhaled treatment
rows: Exacerbations with eosinophilia or concurrent asthma

copd.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [GOLD 2026](https://goldcopd.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/GOLD-REPORT-2026-v1.3-8Dec2025_WMV2.pdf); acute ventilatory care: established teaching.

corticosteroids.name: Corticosteroids
corticosteroids.scope: Mechanism, adverse effects (demargination, leukocytosis, hyperglycemia, osteoporosis, avascular necrosis, steroid myopathy, HPA suppression)
corticosteroids.core: Glucocorticoids rapidly control inflammation and replace deficient cortisol; systemic toxicity depends on cumulative exposure, potency, and duration.

rows.label: Use
items: Prednisone/methylprednisolone: asthma exacerbation, autoimmune flares, transplant rejection
Hydrocortisone: adrenal crisis; dexamethasone: cerebral edema; betamethasone: fetal lung maturation

rows.label: Mechanism
items: Intracellular receptor → altered gene transcription; suppress NF-κB, cytokines, phospholipase A2 pathways
Reduced leukocyte trafficking and lymphocyte activation; slower onset than bronchodilators

rows.label: Adverse
items: ★ **Demargination → neutrophilic leukocytosis**; ↓lymphocytes/eosinophils, ↑glucose/BP, edema
★ **Osteoporosis, avascular necrosis**, painless proximal weakness; cataracts/glaucoma, thin skin
Infection, psychosis, Cushingoid appearance; **HPA suppression** → withdrawal adrenal crisis

rows.label: Avoid
items: Uncontrolled systemic fungal infection; weigh benefit before exposure to tuberculosis or Strongyloides
Live vaccines: defer during prednisone **≥20 mg/day for ≥14 days**; inhaled steroids usually acceptable

rows.label: Interactions
items: NSAIDs → gastrointestinal bleeding; ritonavir/azole antifungals → increased steroid exposure
Rifampin → reduced glucocorticoid effect; adjust diabetes treatment for rising glucose

rows.label: Monitor
items: BP, weight, glucose, infections; chronic use → eye examination and fracture-risk assessment
★ Systemic use ≥3 months → **calcium/vitamin D**; elevated fracture risk → bisphosphonate
Rinse mouth/use spacer with inhaled steroids to prevent thrush

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **<3–4 weeks systemic treatment: usually no taper**; longer courses → taper after disease control
Unconfirmed HPA recovery plus major illness/surgery → stress-dose hydrocortisone
Steroid myopathy: normal CK; new hip pain → MRI for osteonecrosis despite normal radiograph

cranial-nerve-palsies.name: Cranial nerve palsies
cranial-nerve-palsies.scope: CN III palsy, CN IV palsy, CN VI palsy, Bell palsy (CN VII, hyperacusis, corticosteroids), microvascular diabetic neuropathy, cavernous sinus thrombosis
cranial-nerve-palsies.core: Localize diplopia by the weak extraocular muscle; distinguish peripheral facial paralysis from a central lesion by forehead involvement.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Diabetes, hypertension → ischemic mononeuropathy; trauma → trochlear injury
Sinusitis or facial infection → cavernous sinus thrombosis; pregnancy associated with Bell palsy

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **CN III/IV/VI palsy + V1/V2 numbness, proptosis** → cavernous sinus lesion; fever, chemosis → thrombosis
Bell palsy: unilateral upper/lower facial weakness, altered taste, hyperacusis; no other focal deficits
Raised ICP may produce unilateral or bilateral abducens palsy

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Diabetic ischemia often spares superficial parasympathetic CN III fibers; compression threatens pupil function
CN VII inflammation within facial canal disrupts facial movement and stapedius innervation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Acute CN III palsy → urgent **CTA/MRA**, especially painful or pupil-involving; exclude aneurysm
Typical isolated Bell palsy: clinical; atypical/recurrent palsy → MRI, targeted Lyme testing
Suspected cavernous thrombosis → contrast MRI/MRV or CT venography; blood cultures
Isolated diabetic microvascular CN VI palsy: **brain MRI usually normal**

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Bell palsy within 72 hours → **prednisone**; add valacyclovir for severe paralysis
★ Artificial tears, nighttime ointment and eyelid taping to protect exposed cornea
Cavernous thrombosis: IV vancomycin + ceftriaxone + metronidazole; source drainage, consider anticoagulation
Microvascular palsy: vascular risk control, temporary patch/prism; reassess if persistent or progressive

rows.label: Complications
items: Exposure keratitis, corneal ulceration; facial synkinesis after recovery
Septic thrombosis → meningitis, stroke, blindness

rows.label: Prevention
items: Treat facial/sinus infections; optimize diabetes and BP

rows.label: Mimics
items: Stroke: forehead relatively spared with contralateral limb findings
Myasthenia: fatigable variable weakness, normal pupils
Ramsay Hunt: ear vesicles and otalgia with facial paralysis
Carotid-cavernous fistula: post-traumatic **pulsatile proptosis, orbital bruit**, chemosis

table.title: Ocular localization
rows: Worse downstairs; compensatory opposite head tilt

cranial-nerve-palsies.evidence: Not checked online; established neuro-ophthalmology and Bell palsy teaching.

craniosynostosis.name: Craniosynostosis
craniosynostosis.scope: Sagittal synostosis (scaphocephaly), coronal synostosis (anterior plagiocephaly), metopic synostosis, differentiation from positional plagiocephaly, head CT, surgical cranial vault reconstruction
craniosynostosis.core: Persistent abnormal infant head shape from premature fusion of one or more cranial sutures.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Often isolated; multisuture disease or midface hypoplasia suggests a craniofacial syndrome

rows.label: Clues
items: Abnormal shape often present at birth and progresses; palpable ridge over fused suture
Normal head circumference does not exclude single-suture disease because growth continues at open sutures

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Growth restricted perpendicular to fused suture; compensatory expansion along patent sutures

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Examine from above; plot head circumference and assess sutures, orbits and ear position
★ Refer early to craniofacial team; low-dose **3D head CT** when uncertain or for operative planning
Isolated metopic ridge with otherwise normal forehead shape usually physiologic

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Early endoscopic suturectomy with postoperative helmet in selected young infants
★ Open **cranial vault reconstruction** for later presentation or anatomy unsuitable for endoscopic repair

rows.label: Complications
items: Raised intracranial pressure, papilledema, visual impairment, developmental concerns; higher risk with multisuture fusion

rows.label: Mimics
items: ★ Positional plagiocephaly: occipital flattening, ipsilateral anterior ear and frontal bossing; parallelogram from above
Positional dolichocephaly: elongated head in preterm infant without sagittal ridge or biparietal narrowing

craniosynostosis.evidence: Checked AAP clinical report on misshapen head and craniosynostosis (2020).

croup.name: Croup
croup.scope: Parainfluenza virus, barking cough, inspiratory stridor, hoarseness, steeple sign, Westley score, nebulized epinephrine, dexamethasone
croup.core: A toddler with a viral prodrome develops a barking cough, hoarseness, and inspiratory stridor from subglottic airway narrowing.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Usually 6 months–3 years; parainfluenza most common, other respiratory viruses possible
Autumn/winter exposure, daycare; recurrent or atypical-age episodes suggest structural airway disease

rows.label: Clues
items: Symptoms often worsen at night; low-grade fever, retractions, agitation with respiratory distress
★ **Stridor at rest** marks clinically significant obstruction; cyanosis/lethargy suggests impending failure
Drooling, tripod posture, toxicity, or high fever → reconsider diagnosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Viral laryngotracheal inflammation causes edema within the rigid cricoid ring
Small reductions in pediatric airway radius produce large increases in airflow resistance

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis**; routine imaging, viral testing, and blood draws unnecessary
AP neck x-ray: steeple-shaped subglottic narrowing, supportive but neither required nor specific
Westley: stridor, retractions, air entry, cyanosis, consciousness; 0–2 mild, 3–7 moderate, ≥8 severe

rows.label: Tx
items: Keep child calm with caregiver; oxygen if hypoxemic; avoid unnecessary upsetting procedures
★ **Dexamethasone once for all severities**; oral route preferred when tolerated
★ Moderate/severe disease → **nebulized epinephrine**; observe ≥2–3 hours after last dose
Persistent resting symptoms, repeated epinephrine, poor intake → admit; exhaustion/hypoxia → expert airway management
No routine antibiotics, bronchodilators, or cough suppressants; humidified air lacks proven benefit

rows.label: Complications
items: Respiratory failure, dehydration; rare secondary bacterial tracheitis
Epinephrine effect wears off before steroid benefit; reassess rather than discharge immediately

rows.label: Prevention
items: Hand hygiene, respiratory etiquette, reduced close contact during acute viral illness

rows.label: Mimics
items: Epiglottitis: drooling, dysphagia, muffled voice, tripod posture; secure airway without throat manipulation
Bacterial tracheitis: toxic, high fever, thick secretions, poor epinephrine response
Foreign body: abrupt choking, no preceding viral syndrome

croup.evidence: Not checked online; established pediatric emergency teaching.

decompression-illness.name: Decompression illness
decompression-illness.scope: Decompression sickness, arterial gas embolism, hyperbaric oxygen therapy
decompression-illness.core: Symptoms after surfacing can reflect nitrogen bubbles or pulmonary-barotrauma air emboli; immediate oxygen and urgent recompression prevent permanent injury.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Rapid ascent, deep/prolonged/repetitive dives, inadequate decompression, altitude exposure soon after diving
Breath-holding during ascent increases pulmonary barotrauma; right-to-left shunt facilitates systemic bubbles

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Any focal neurologic deficit after diving** → treat as decompression emergency
Joint pain, pruritic mottled skin, vertigo, weakness, urinary retention or dyspnea
Confusion, seizure or loss of consciousness immediately after ascent strongly suggests arterial embolism

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Falling ambient pressure releases dissolved inert gas into tissues/blood
Expanding trapped pulmonary gas can rupture alveoli and enter arterial circulation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis** from dive profile and symptom timing; normal imaging does not exclude
Neurologic examination, pulse oximetry, ECG; chest imaging for suspected pneumothorax
Do not delay hyperbaric referral for CT/MRI or laboratory confirmation
Distinguish inner-ear barotrauma from vestibular decompression illness with specialist assessment

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **100% oxygen**, airway support, isotonic IV fluids; urgent hyperbaric-medicine consultation
★ **Hyperbaric oxygen recompression** for arterial gas embolism or significant decompression sickness
Supine positioning; no Trendelenburg, no in-water recompression or nitrous oxide
Treat pneumothorax before chamber pressurization; transport at lowest feasible altitude

rows.label: Complications
items: Spinal cord injury, paralysis, persistent vestibular dysfunction, cognitive deficits or death
Recurrent/prolonged pressure exposure → dysbaric osteonecrosis; delayed treatment worsens neurologic recovery

rows.label: Prevention
items: Controlled ascent and safety stops; avoid breath-holding and dehydration
Wait ≥12 hours after one no-decompression dive, ≥18 hours after repetitive dives before flying

rows.label: Mimics
items: Pulmonary barotrauma: pleuritic pain, pneumothorax without required systemic embolization
Stroke: vascular syndrome without pressure exposure; immersion pulmonary edema: water-associated respiratory distress

depressive-disorders.name: Depressive disorders
depressive-disorders.scope: Major depressive disorder criteria, depression in older adults, bereavement vs MDD, pharmacotherapy, psychotherapy, suicide risk
depressive-disorders.core: Persistent low mood or loss of pleasure with neurovegetative and cognitive symptoms, causing clinically significant distress or impaired function.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior episodes, family history, chronic illness/pain, substance use, postpartum period, social isolation
Older adults: disability, bereavement, polypharmacy; somatic presentations

rows.label: Clues
items: SIGECAPS: sleep, interest, guilt, energy, concentration, appetite, psychomotor change, suicidality
Psychotic depression: delusions/hallucinations only during mood episodes, often guilt or nihilism
★ **Suicide risk**: prior attempt, intent, plan, means, agitation, psychosis, intoxication
Youth: **irritable mood** qualifies; academic decline, withdrawal, somatic complaints; not normal teenage behavior

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Multifactorial mood-circuit dysfunction involving monoamines, **HPA hyperactivity with raised cortisol**, and neuroplasticity

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ MDD: **≥5 symptoms for ≥2 weeks**, including depressed mood or anhedonia; exclude mania/hypomania
Screen all adults, even asymptomatic: PHQ-2, PHQ-9 for severity; older adults: **Geriatric Depression Scale**
Interview establishes diagnosis; assess substances, drugs, TSH/CBC when clinically suspected
★ **Ask directly about suicide**, access to firearms, protective factors; questioning does not increase risk
Post-CABG anhedonia, withdrawal, fatigue → depression screen; vein-harvest leg edema expected

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Imminent danger or **severe malnutrition** → **observation, psychiatric hospitalization**; remove lethal means
Mild: CBT/interpersonal therapy; moderate/severe: sertraline + psychotherapy; pregnancy → shared risk–benefit discussion
★ Urgent suicidality/catatonia/anorexia → **ECT**; psychotic depression → ECT or antidepressant + antipsychotic
Alternatives: **bupropion** (fatigue/hypersomnia, smoking cessation), **mirtazapine** (poor appetite, insomnia)
Continue antidepressant ≥6 months after remission; recurrent/severe episodes → longer maintenance

rows.label: Complications
items: Suicide, malnutrition, functional decline, recurrence
SSRIs: sexual dysfunction, GI effects, hyponatremia; early activation/suicidality monitoring, especially age <25
Bupropion: seizures; avoid with eating disorders, seizure disorders or brain tumor; mirtazapine: weight gain/sedation
Benzodiazepines in older adults: worsen depression, sedation, falls → stop, use antidepressant

rows.label: Prevention
items: Safety plan, early follow-up after drug changes
Taper antidepressants to reduce discontinuation symptoms; avoid antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar disorder

rows.label: Mimics
items: Dementia: insidious consistent deficits; **pseudodementia**: subacute, "I don't know" answers, recall improves with prompting
Hypothyroidism: cold intolerance, constipation, elevated TSH
Untreated OSA: snoring, obesity, sleepiness → **mood disorder due to medical condition**, not MDD
Anorexia nervosa: fear of weight gain, distorted body image

table.title: Distinguishing persistent sadness
rows: Waves tied to reminders; self-esteem usually preserved
Pervasive worthlessness; bereavement does not exclude diagnosis
Stressor within 3 months; MDD criteria absent

dermatophyte-infections.name: Dermatophyte infections
dermatophyte-infections.scope: Tinea capitis, tinea corporis, tinea pedis, tinea cruris, onychomycosis, potassium hydroxide preparation, oral and topical antifungals
dermatophyte-infections.core: Keratin-invading fungi cause scaly skin lesions or infected hair/nails; the anatomic site determines topical versus systemic treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Warm humid conditions, occlusive footwear, shared showers, wrestling, infected animals or contacts
Diabetes, immunosuppression; childhood favors scalp infection; nail disease increases with age

rows.label: Clues
items: Pruritus and peripheral scaling; steroid exposure may distort borders and suppress inflammation
★ **Boggy tender scalp plaque** → kerion; inflammatory disease risks permanent scarring alopecia
Interdigital maceration/fissures can become bacterial entry sites

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Trichophyton, Microsporum, Epidermophyton digest keratin in stratum corneum, hair, and nails
**T rubrum** most common on skin/nails; capitis → **T tonsurans** (endothrix)
Follicular/deep involvement prevents topical agents from reaching the infected reservoir

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **KOH preparation of active edge** → branching septate hyphae; obtain before systemic treatment when uncertain
Scalp: hair/plucked scale microscopy and culture; nail: clipping KOH, PAS, or fungal culture
Wood lamp detects only selected organisms; negative fluorescence does not exclude tinea
Refractory/widespread infection → reassess diagnosis, adherence, resistance; fungal culture can guide further care

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Limited skin disease → **topical terbinafine** or clotrimazole; continue beyond clinical clearing
★ Hair infection → **oral griseofulvin or terbinafine**; adjunct selenium sulfide/ketoconazole shampoo reduces spread
Nail infection → confirm fungus, then oral terbinafine; baseline liver assessment; counsel slow regrowth
Avoid topical corticosteroid monotherapy or steroid-antifungal combinations; extensive disease may require oral antifungal

rows.label: Complications
items: Secondary cellulitis, persistent nail dystrophy, recurrent infection from untreated reservoirs
Oral antifungals: hepatotoxicity, drug interactions; griseofulvin contraindicated during pregnancy

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Keep feet dry**, change socks, avoid shared towels/combs, disinfect sports gear
Treat symptomatic contacts/pets and coexisting tinea pedis (autoinfects groin → recurrence); avoid barefoot communal-shower exposure

rows.label: Mimics
items: Candida intertrigo: satellite pustules, scrotal involvement
Psoriasis: sharply demarcated plaques, nail pitting; alopecia areata: smooth nonscaly patches

table.title: Site clues
rows: Broken hairs, black dots, patchy alopecia, occipital nodes
Annular plaque, advancing border, central clearing
Thick yellow brittle nail, subungual debris

dermatophyte-infections.evidence: Not checked online; established dermatophyte diagnosis and site-based treatment.

diagnostic-test-accuracy.name: Diagnostic test accuracy
diagnostic-test-accuracy.scope: Sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, likelihood ratios, cut-off changes
diagnostic-test-accuracy.core: Diagnostic accuracy: classification performance against a reference standard; distinguish detection ability from the probability that a result reflects disease.

rows.label: Definition
items: TP/FP: diseased/nondiseased testing positive; FN/TN: diseased/nondiseased testing negative
False negatives → low sensitivity, an intrinsic test property; NPV varies with prevalence

rows.label: Interpret
items: ★ ↑Prevalence → **↑PPV, ↓NPV**; sensitivity/specificity unchanged if disease spectrum unchanged
★ Positive above threshold: **lower cutoff → ↑sensitivity, ↓specificity**; raising cutoff reverses
LR+ >10 rules in; LR− <0.1 rules out; **LR 1** → no information

rows.label: Use when
items: ★ Pretest odds = p/(1−p); **posttest odds = pretest odds × LR**
Posttest probability = odds/(1+odds); pretest 20%, LR+ 4 → odds 1 → 50%
Parallel tests, either positive → ↑sensitivity; serial tests, both positive → ↑specificity

rows.label: Compare
items: ROC: sensitivity versus 1−specificity; AUC 0.5 = chance, 1 = perfect
ROC point nearest **upper-left corner** → best combined sensitivity and specificity

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Sensitive negative** helps exclude; specific positive helps confirm; neither absolute
Case-control sampling → PPV/NPV unrepresentative without population prevalence
Verification bias: reference testing only selected results → distorted accuracy

diagnostic-test-accuracy.evidence: Established statistical definitions; no guideline-dependent recommendation.

drug-induced-liver-injury.name: Drug-induced liver injury
drug-induced-liver-injury.scope: Idiosyncratic DILI, culprit drugs (TMP-SMX, augmentin, isoniazid, nitrofurantoin), hepatocellular vs cholestatic injury, drug discontinuation, acute liver failure criteria
drug-induced-liver-injury.core: New hepatitis or cholestasis temporally linked to a medication or supplement after competing causes are excluded.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Amoxicillin-clavulanate and TMP-SMX: often cholestatic or mixed
Isoniazid: hepatocellular; nitrofurantoin: acute hepatitis or chronic autoimmune-like injury

rows.label: Clues
items: Malaise, nausea, jaundice, pruritus; fever, rash or eosinophilia suggest hypersensitivity
Delayed onset after completion possible, especially with amoxicillin-clavulanate

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Idiosyncratic injury: unpredictable host susceptibility, often immune-mediated; acetaminophen toxicity is dose-dependent

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **R ratio** = (ALT/ULN) ÷ (ALP/ULN), using values at presentation
Review medication timing and supplements; test for viral hepatitis, autoimmune hepatitis, acetaminophen exposure
Ultrasound for biliary obstruction; trend bilirubin and INR
★ **Acute liver failure**: INR ≥1.5 plus encephalopathy within 26 weeks without preexisting cirrhosis

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Stop culprit promptly**; generally avoid rechallenge
★ Acute liver failure → urgent transplant center evaluation
N-acetylcysteine for acetaminophen toxicity and selected early non-acetaminophen acute liver failure

rows.label: Complications
items: Hepatocellular injury plus bilirubin >2× ULN without obstruction or other cause → higher mortality risk
Persistent cholestasis, chronic hepatitis, transplantation or death

rows.label: Prevention
items: Document culprit, counsel on recurrence and report serious suspected reactions

rows.label: Mimics
items: Choledocholithiasis: ductal stone or dilation on imaging
Ischemic hepatitis: abrupt marked aminotransferase rise after hypoperfusion

drug-induced-liver-injury.evidence: Checked AASLD practice guidance on drug, herbal and dietary supplement-induced liver injury (2023).

dyslipidemia.name: Dyslipidemia
dyslipidemia.scope: Lipid screening guidelines, ASCVD risk calculation, statin therapy indications, monitoring response to diet and pharmacotherapy
dyslipidemia.core: Excess atherogenic lipoproteins drive ASCVD; treatment intensity follows established disease, severe LDL elevation, diabetes, and estimated absolute cardiovascular risk.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Familial disorders, saturated-fat intake, obesity, diabetes, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, cholestasis
Premature ASCVD family history, CKD, smoking, inflammatory disease increase treatment benefit

rows.label: Clues
items: Usually asymptomatic; tendon xanthomas/early corneal arcus suggest familial hypercholesterolemia
Severe triglyceride elevation: eruptive xanthomas, pancreatitis; low HDL alone is not a drug target

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Retained apoB-containing particles → arterial inflammation and plaque formation
Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase → hepatic LDL-receptor upregulation
Familial hypercholesterolemia: **defective LDL-receptor uptake** → isolated high LDL, clear plasma; high TG: milky plasma

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Lipid panel from age 19, at least every 5 years**; earlier/more often with risk
Nonfasting panel acceptable; markedly high triglycerides → fasting repeat/secondary-cause evaluation; Lp(a) once/lifetime
★ **PREVENT-ASCVD**, ages 30–79, LDL 70–189 without ASCVD: replaces pooled-cohort equations in 2026 guidance
Uncertain statin decision → coronary calcium; zero insufficient for deferral with diabetes, smoking, strong premature history
High total cholesterol alone → full lipid panel before treatment

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Clinical ASCVD (CAD, stroke, PAD) or **LDL ≥190 mg/dL → high-intensity statin**, no risk calculation required
★ Diabetes age 40–75 → **at least moderate-intensity statin**; multiple risk factors favor high intensity
Above LDL target despite maximal statin → ezetimibe; consider PCSK9 inhibitor or bempedoic acid
Severe triglycerides ≥500 → address causes, diet, consider fenofibrate/prescription omega-3 to reduce pancreatitis risk
Adolescent obesity + moderate LDL → **calorie reduction/lifestyle first**; statin only if severe or persistent

rows.label: Complications
items: MI, stroke, peripheral arterial disease; statins → myalgias, rare rhabdomyolysis, small diabetes-risk increase
Baseline ALT; CK only with symptoms/risk; most lipid-lowering drugs deferred during conception/pregnancy/lactation

rows.label: Prevention
items: Mediterranean-style diet, replace saturated fats, exercise, weight reduction, smoking cessation
★ Recheck lipids **4–12 weeks after diet/drug change**, then every 3–12 months; high despite diet → statin
High intensity lowers LDL ≥50%: atorvastatin 40–80 mg or rosuvastatin 20–40 mg

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hypothyroidism: elevated TSH; correct before labeling primary dyslipidemia
Nephrotic syndrome: heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia; treat renal cause

table.title: Risk-based primary prevention and secondary target

dyspepsia-and-peptic-ulcer-disease.name: Dyspepsia and peptic ulcer disease
dyspepsia-and-peptic-ulcer-disease.scope: Uninvestigated dyspepsia (age < 60 test-and-treat vs age >= 60 endoscopy), Helicobacter pylori testing and eradication, gastric and duodenal ulcers
dyspepsia-and-peptic-ulcer-disease.core: Epigastric discomfort may reflect functional dyspepsia or acid-peptic ulceration; age and bleeding risk determine noninvasive testing versus endoscopy.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: H pylori, NSAIDs/aspirin; smoking impairs healing
Prior ulcer bleeding, anticoagulants, older age amplify NSAID harm; severe physiologic stress causes ICU ulcers

rows.label: Clues
items: Epigastric burning, early satiety, nausea; meal timing cannot reliably distinguish ulcer location
★ **Alarm**: hematemesis/melena, positive occult blood, dysphagia, persistent vomiting, weight loss, iron-deficiency anemia
Sudden rigid abdomen → perforation
Early satiety, nonbilious vomiting, succussion splash, gastric distention → gastric outlet obstruction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: H pylori or prostaglandin depletion weakens mucosal defenses against acid-pepsin injury
Antral-predominant infection increases acid; corpus-predominant inflammation may cause atrophy

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ New dyspepsia **≥60 years or any alarm feature → upper endoscopy**
★ Under 60 without concerning features → **urea breath or stool antigen test**
Hold PPI 2 weeks and antibiotics/bismuth 4 weeks before active-infection testing; serology cannot confirm eradication
Gastric ulcer → biopsy to exclude malignancy; duodenal ulcers rarely malignant
Refractory/recurrent multiple ulcers + diarrhea → fasting gastrin with careful PPI interpretation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ H pylori → **14-day bismuth quadruple**: PPI + bismuth + tetracycline + metronidazole
Avoid empiric clarithromycin/levofloxacin regimens unless susceptibility demonstrated
Negative infection test or persistent symptoms after eradication → PPI trial; functional symptoms may need TCA
Stop NSAID; ulcer healing → PPI; active bleeding → resuscitation, IV PPI, urgent endoscopic hemostasis
Perforation → IV fluids, ceftriaxone/metronidazole, urgent surgery; no elective diagnostic endoscopy

rows.label: Complications
items: Hemorrhage, perforation, penetration, outlet obstruction from scarring/fibrosis; H pylori → gastric cancer, MALT lymphoma

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Confirm eradication ≥4 weeks after antibiotics** with breath/stool test, off PPI as above
Necessary NSAID + high GI risk → concurrent PPI; use lowest effective NSAID exposure

rows.label: Mimics
items: Biliary colic: episodic RUQ pain, gallstones on ultrasound
ACS: exertional epigastric pressure, ischemic ECG/troponin findings

dyspepsia-and-peptic-ulcer-disease.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ACG H pylori update (2024)](https://gi.org/journals-publications/ebgi/schoenfeld_sep2024/); dyspepsia age threshold established ACG/CAG teaching.

eating-disorders.name: Eating disorders
eating-disorders.scope: Anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, binge eating disorder, refeeding syndrome, medical complications, hospitalization criteria
eating-disorders.core: Disordered intake or compensatory behaviors require assessment of medical instability, suicidality, and malnutrition at any body size.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Adolescence, dieting, weight stigma, perfectionism, trauma; psychiatric comorbidity and family history

rows.label: Clues
items: Restrictive disease: cold intolerance, lanugo, bradycardia, orthostasis, menstrual suppression; amenorrhea not required
Purging: parotid hypertrophy, **raised amylase**, enamel erosion, knuckle calluses; hypokalemic hypochloremic alkalosis
★ **Syncope, arrhythmia, hypothermia or severe electrolyte abnormalities** → urgent stabilization

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Starvation suppresses gonadal axis and reduces cardiac mass; vomiting causes chloride/volume depletion
Refeeding insulin surge shifts phosphate, potassium and magnesium intracellularly

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Clinical interview plus weight trajectory, vitals/orthostatics, **ECG, electrolytes, Mg, phosphate**
Binge: loss of control plus unusually large intake; bulimia/BED require episodes ≥weekly for 3 months
Assess suicide risk, substance use, exercise, laxatives; normal BMI does not exclude severe disease

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Medical admission for instability: e.g., HR <50, BP <90/60, severe electrolyte disturbance or acute food refusal
★ Refeeding → **thiamine**, nutritional rehabilitation, serial phosphate/K/Mg and cardiac monitoring
Adolescent anorexia → family-based treatment; adults → eating-disorder-focused psychotherapy; medication alone insufficient
Bulimia → CBT plus fluoxetine; avoid bupropion because of seizures
BED → CBT; lisdexamfetamine for selected adults, monitor misuse/cardiovascular risk

rows.label: Complications
items: Hypoestrogenism → osteoporosis, infertility; cardiac failure, arrhythmic death; purging → arrhythmias, esophageal injury
Refeeding → hypophosphatemia, respiratory failure, edema, delirium; high suicide mortality
Severe starvation → **hypoalbuminemia** with pitting edema

rows.label: Prevention
items: Early recognition of growth/weight-trajectory changes; reduce weight-based stigma; relapse follow-up

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hyperthyroidism: increased appetite with tremor and heat intolerance
GI malabsorption: involuntary weight loss without weight/shape-driven restriction

eating-disorders.evidence: Guideline framework checked 2026-10-30: [APA eating disorders guideline, 2023](https://www.psychiatry.org/psychiatrists/practice/clinical-practice-guidelines/eating-disorders); thresholds: established clinical teaching.

table.title: Diagnostic distinction
rows: Restriction or purging + weight-gain fear/distorted self-image

ectopic-pregnancy.name: Ectopic pregnancy
ectopic-pregnancy.scope: Diagnosis (beta-hCG, transvaginal ultrasound, discriminatory zone), unruptured ectopic pregnancy, medical management (methotrexate), ruptured ectopic pregnancy, surgical management
ectopic-pregnancy.core: Pregnancy implanted outside the endometrial cavity, usually tubal; early pregnancy with pelvic pain or bleeding requires localization and rupture assessment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior ectopic, PID/tubal damage, tubal surgery, infertility treatment, smoking
IUDs prevent pregnancy overall; pregnancy despite IUD has higher ectopic proportion; many cases lack risks

rows.label: Clues
items: Amenorrhea, unilateral pelvic pain, spotting; cervical motion/adnexal tenderness nonspecific
★ **Syncope, shoulder-tip pain, peritoneal signs, hypotension** → hemoperitoneum/rupture
Heterotopic pregnancy possible despite visualized intrauterine pregnancy, particularly after assisted reproduction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Impaired tubal transport → extrauterine trophoblastic implantation, invasion, hemorrhage
Methotrexate inhibits folate-dependent DNA synthesis in proliferating trophoblast

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Pregnancy test → quantitative beta-hCG + transvaginal ultrasound**; ultrasound regardless of hCG when symptomatic
Extrauterine yolk sac/embryo diagnostic; adnexal mass/free fluid supportive; empty uterus alone insufficient
★ Stable pregnancy of unknown location → **repeat hCG in 48 hours**, serial ultrasound until resolved/localized
Subnormal 48-hour hCG rise + empty uterus + pain → suspect **ectopic**; rapid fall favors miscarriage
Discriminatory threshold up to 3,500 mIU/mL protects viable IUP; abnormal rise/fall cannot establish location

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Unstable/rupture concern → **IV access, blood resuscitation, urgent laparotomy**; do not await serial hCG
Confirmed unruptured, stable, reliable follow-up, hCG <5,000, mass <3.5 cm, no fetal heartbeat → consider **methotrexate**
Avoid methotrexate: viable IUP, breastfeeding, hepatic/renal disease, cytopenias, immunodeficiency, unreliable follow-up
Postmethotrexate hCG days 4/7: fall ≥15% → weekly until negative; inadequate fall → reassess/re-dose/surgery

rows.label: Complications
items: Hemorrhagic shock, death, tubal loss, recurrence, impaired fertility
Methotrexate: mucositis, hepatotoxicity, marrow suppression; rupture remains possible despite falling hCG

rows.label: Prevention
items: Treat/prevent STIs, smoking cessation; prior ectopic → early ultrasound in subsequent pregnancy
Methotrexate counseling: avoid alcohol, folate supplements, intercourse until resolution; avoid conception for 3 months
Unsensitized Rh-negative ectopic → Rh(D) immune globulin; provide return precautions for escalating pain/dizziness

rows.label: Mimics
items: Miscarriage: intrauterine pregnancy loss; passage of decidual tissue alone does not prove IUP
Hemorrhagic corpus luteum: ovarian source, may coexist with normal pregnancy
Ovarian torsion: abrupt severe unilateral pain, enlarged ovary

table.title: Alternative definitive branches
rows: Stable, minimal symptoms, low declining hCG
Selected expectant management with reliable surveillance
Heartbeat, high hCG, severe pain, or contraindication

ectopic-pregnancy.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ACOG ectopic pregnancy](https://www.acog.org/womens-health/faqs/ectopic-pregnancy), [NICE tubal ectopic management](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/NG126/chapter/management-of-tubal-ectopic-pregnancy); conservative discriminatory threshold established ACOG teaching.

enterovirus-infections.name: Enterovirus infections
enterovirus-infections.scope: Coxsackievirus A, Coxsackievirus B (epidemic pleurodynia, viral myocarditis, pericarditis), echovirus, aseptic meningitis
enterovirus-infections.core: Enteroviruses cause common self-limited febrile syndromes but also aseptic meningitis, myocarditis and severe neonatal sepsis-like illness.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Young children, summer/early autumn, childcare exposure; fecal–oral and respiratory spread
Newborn peripartum exposure and antibody deficiency increase severe disseminated infection risk

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Hand-foot-mouth: oral ulcers plus **vesicles on palms/soles**; sometimes buttocks
Herpangina: fever with painful **posterior oropharyngeal vesicles/ulcers**, usually no hand/foot eruption
Pleurodynia: paroxysmal chest/upper abdominal muscle spasms, fever, **elevated CK**
Neonates: poor feeding, hepatitis, coagulopathy, shock or arrhythmia; older children: headache/meningismus

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Nonenveloped positive-sense RNA picornaviruses survive gastric acidity; replication followed by viremia
Tissue tropism produces mucocutaneous, meningeal, myocardial or skeletal muscle disease

rows.label: Dx
items: Typical uncomplicated exanthem → clinical diagnosis; no routine serology
★ Suspected meningitis → **LP with CSF enterovirus PCR**, bacterial studies and glucose/protein
Viral CSF usually lymphocytic, normal glucose, mildly elevated protein; early neutrophils possible
Chest pain with cardiac concern → ECG, troponin, echocardiography; MRI for suspected myocarditis
Ill neonate → blood/CSF cultures and sepsis evaluation; do not assume benign viral disease

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Uncomplicated disease → **oral fluids, acetaminophen/ibuprofen**, assess hydration
Unexcluded bacterial meningitis/sepsis → empiric ceftriaxone + vancomycin; neonates → ampicillin + cefotaxime
Myocarditis → cardiac monitoring, heart-failure support; shock → intensive care and circulatory support
No routine antibiotic or antiviral treatment for confirmed uncomplicated enterovirus infection
Painful mouth lesions → cool liquids; avoid aspirin in children

rows.label: Complications
items: Dehydration, myopericarditis, encephalitis; some serotypes cause acute flaccid myelitis
Fulminant neonatal hepatitis/coagulopathy or myocardial failure can be fatal

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Handwashing with soap, surface cleaning, diaper hygiene; viral stool shedding can persist
Routine polio vaccination prevents poliomyelitis; no routine US vaccine for nonpolio enteroviruses

rows.label: Mimics
items: HSV gingivostomatitis: anterior diffuse gingivitis and painful lesions
Bacterial meningitis: low CSF glucose, high protein; cultures/PCR establish cause
Pulmonary embolism: hypoxemia, clot risk; viral pleurisy → fever, **pleural friction rub**, viral rash
Streptococcal pharyngitis: tonsillar exudates, palatal petechiae, no discrete vesicles

enterovirus-infections.evidence: Not checked online; established infectious-disease teaching.

epididymitis.name: Epididymitis
epididymitis.scope: Acute epididymitis, sexually transmitted vs enteric pathogens by age, Prehn sign, empiric antibiotic regimens, ruling out torsion
epididymitis.core: Gradual unilateral posterior testicular pain with urinary or urethral inflammation suggests epididymitis; always assess for torsion first.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Sexually active younger adults: gonorrhea/chlamydia; older adults with obstruction/instrumentation: enteric organisms
Insertive anal intercourse permits both STI and enteric pathogens; exposure matters more than age

rows.label: Clues
items: Tender swollen epididymis, dysuria, fever, possible urethral discharge; cremasteric reflex often preserved
Prehn sign: elevation may relieve pain, but **cannot exclude torsion**
Sudden severe onset, nausea, high-riding/horizontal testis → surgical emergency

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Ascending urethral/urinary infection spreads through vas deferens → epididymal inflammation
Extension into testis causes epididymo-orchitis; edema can impair perfusion in severe disease

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ High torsion suspicion → **urgent urology/exploration**, without waiting for testing
Uncertain → **Doppler ultrasound**; epididymal hyperemia favors infection, absent testicular flow favors torsion
★ First-catch urine **gonorrhea/chlamydia NAAT**, urinalysis, bacterial urine culture; HIV/syphilis testing
Negative ultrasound does not exclude epididymitis; persistent mass warrants alternative-diagnosis evaluation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Empiric antibiotics after specimens; **scrotal support, NSAIDs**, relative rest
Treat before test results; regimen determined by likely pathogens, not age alone
Reevaluate if no improvement within **72 hours**; severe fever/pain or inability to adhere → hospitalization

rows.label: Complications
items: Abscess, testicular infarction, chronic scrotal pain, reduced fertility
Persistent swelling after treatment → assess tumor, TB, abscess, infarction

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ STI-associated infection: **partners from prior 60 days** need evaluation/presumptive treatment
Abstain until both partners treated and symptoms resolved; condoms reduce reinfection

rows.label: Mimics
items: Testicular torsion: abrupt pain, absent reflex; urgent detorsion required
Torsed appendage: focal upper-pole tenderness, blue-dot sign
Inguinal hernia: groin/scrotal mass, bowel symptoms, reducibility or strangulation

esophageal-motility-disorders.name: Esophageal motility disorders
esophageal-motility-disorders.scope: Achalasia, diffuse esophageal spasm, hypercontractile esophagus, Zenker diverticulum, manometry, barium swallow
esophageal-motility-disorders.core: Dysphagia to solids and liquids from onset suggests impaired motility; progressive solids-first dysphagia suggests mechanical obstruction.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Achalasia often idiopathic; Chagas disease can destroy enteric ganglia
Older age predisposes to Zenker diverticulum; opioids can produce spastic motility patterns

rows.label: Clues
items: Achalasia: regurgitated undigested food, nocturnal cough, weight loss
★ Zenker: **halitosis, cervical gurgling, aspiration**, retained food hours after eating
Spastic disorders: intermittent dysphagia and squeezing chest pain; hot/cold liquids may provoke

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Achalasia: loss of inhibitory myenteric neurons → impaired LES relaxation and absent peristalsis
Zenker: cricopharyngeal dysfunction → mucosal herniation through Killian triangle

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Esophageal symptoms → **upper endoscopy** to exclude stricture/cancer before motility testing
★ **High-resolution manometry** confirms functional disorder after structural disease excluded
Barium swallow defines emptying; suspected Zenker → **barium study before endoscopy**
Rapid weight loss, older onset or difficult LES passage → evaluate pseudoachalasia with CT/endoscopic ultrasound
Chest pain → exclude ACS before labeling esophageal spasm

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Achalasia → pneumatic dilation, Heller myotomy + fundoplication, or **POEM**
Botulinum toxin for achalasia when procedural risk precludes durable treatment
Spastic disorders → remove opioid trigger, treat reflux; diltiazem or nitrates for persistent symptoms
Symptomatic Zenker → **cricopharyngeal myotomy + diverticulectomy** or endoscopic septotomy; no dilation or blind NG tube

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration pneumonia, malnutrition; longstanding achalasia → increased squamous cancer risk
Dilation/myotomy → perforation; myotomy, especially POEM → gastroesophageal reflux

rows.label: Prevention
items: Eat slowly, chew thoroughly, remain upright after meals to reduce regurgitation/aspiration

rows.label: Mimics
items: Esophageal cancer: progressive solids-first symptoms; obstructing lesion
Scleroderma: hypotensive LES with reflux, distal aperistalsis

table.title: Manometry and contrast findings
rows: Impaired LES relaxation; absent normal peristalsis

esophageal-motility-disorders.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ACG achalasia guideline](https://gi.org/guideline/diagnosis-and-management-of-achalasia/); other disorders established teaching.

essential-hypertension.name: Essential hypertension
essential-hypertension.scope: Blood pressure staging, nonpharmacologic interventions (weight loss, DASH, exercise), first-line antihypertensive agents, resistant hypertension
essential-hypertension.core: Persistently elevated arterial pressure usually reflects multifactorial primary hypertension; confirm accurate repeated measurements before long-term treatment decisions.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age, family history, obesity, excess sodium/alcohol, inactivity, poor sleep
NSAIDs, stimulants, oral contraceptives can raise BP; assess before labeling primary disease

rows.label: Clues
items: Usually asymptomatic; headache alone does not establish hypertensive emergency
★ **Acute target-organ injury** with severe pressure → hypertensive emergency; BP number alone insufficient

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Increased vascular resistance, altered renal sodium handling, sympathetic/RAAS activation sustain elevated pressure
Chronic endothelial injury accelerates atherosclerosis and small-vessel organ damage
Older adults: large-artery stiffness (low compliance) → **isolated systolic hypertension**, wide pulse pressure

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Average ≥2 readings on ≥2 visits; confirm using **home BP or ambulatory monitoring**
Rest seated, feet supported, correct cuff, arm at heart level; avoid recent caffeine/exercise
BMP, creatinine/eGFR, urinalysis/albuminuria, lipids, glucose/A1c, ECG assess risk and injury
Resistant: above goal on 3 agents including diuretic, or controlled on ≥4; exclude pseudoresistance
Child/adolescent high oscillometric reading → **confirm by auscultation** before ambulatory monitoring or workup

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **DASH diet, weight reduction, sodium restriction, aerobic activity**, moderate alcohol; target generally <130/80
≥140/90 → drugs, usually two classes; ≥130/80 with CVD, diabetes, CKD, or PREVENT ≥7.5% → drugs
★ Low-risk stage 1: **3–6 months lifestyle**, then drugs if still ≥130/80; updated 2025 threshold
Initial: chlorthalidone, amlodipine, lisinopril, or losartan; albuminuric CKD → ACE inhibitor/ARB (older exams: any diabetes)
Resistant after optimized triple regimen → spironolactone; monitor K/creatinine; never combine ACE inhibitor + ARB

rows.label: Complications
items: Stroke, MI, LV hypertrophy/HF, CKD, retinopathy, aortic disease
Thiazide: low Na/K, gout; ACE inhibitor: cough/angioedema; RAAS drugs contraindicated in pregnancy

rows.label: Prevention
items: Medication adherence, home readings, regular follow-up; assess orthostatic symptoms in older adults
Weight loss: largest lifestyle BP drop, ~1 mm Hg/kg; smoking cessation barely lowers resting BP
BP control: largest modifiable stroke-risk reduction; also prevents concentric LVH and HF

rows.label: Mimics
items: White-coat hypertension: office high, home normal
Masked hypertension: elevated out-of-office only; secondary causes: abrupt/refractory pressure with renal/endocrine clues

essential-tremor.name: Essential tremor
essential-tremor.scope: Postural and kinetic bilateral action tremor, hands and head tremor, alcohol responsiveness, absence of parkinsonian features, propranolol, primidone, topiramate, deep brain stimulation
essential-tremor.core: Gradual bilateral hand shaking during posture or action, often with a familial pattern and temporary improvement after alcohol.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Family history often autosomal dominant; prevalence rises with age

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Action tremor**, impaired writing/pouring; head or voice may also be affected
No bradykinesia, rigidity, focal weakness, sensory loss or cerebellar gait dysfunction
Usually symmetric; finger-to-nose tremor without true dysmetria

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Abnormal oscillation within cerebellothalamocortical networks; no single routine diagnostic biomarker

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical examination**: observe rest, outstretched arms, handwriting/spiral drawing and goal-directed movement
Review beta-agonists, stimulants, lithium, valproate; TSH if hyperthyroidism possible
MRI reserved for abrupt onset, focal deficits, marked asymmetry or other atypical features

rows.label: Tx
items: Mild symptoms → reassurance, adaptive utensils, reduce triggers
★ Function-limiting hand tremor → **propranolol or primidone**; combination if partial response
Propranolol: avoid with asthma, symptomatic bradycardia or heart block; primidone: sedation/ataxia
Persistent symptoms → topiramate; selected head/voice tremor → botulinum toxin
★ Severe drug-refractory disability → **thalamic DBS** or selected focused ultrasound thalamotomy

rows.label: Complications
items: Difficulty eating, writing, grooming; social embarrassment and occupational limitations
Treatment-related fatigue, hypotension, cognitive slowing; botulinum toxin can cause focal weakness

rows.label: Prevention
items: No established disease prevention; minimize caffeine and sleep deprivation to reduce exacerbations
Avoid alcohol as chronic treatment because of dependence and rebound symptoms

rows.label: Mimics
items: Parkinson disease: asymmetric resting tremor, bradykinesia and rigidity
Enhanced physiologic tremor: fine, trigger-related; resolves with cause correction
Cerebellar tremor: intention worsening with dysmetria, nystagmus or ataxia

essential-tremor.evidence: Not checked online; established movement-disorder diagnosis and treatment teaching.

foreign-body-aspiration.name: Foreign body aspiration
foreign-body-aspiration.scope: Pediatric airway foreign body, choking maneuvers, rigid bronchoscopy, chest x-ray findings (air trapping, atelectasis), observation of partial obstruction
foreign-body-aspiration.core: Abrupt choking with unilateral wheeze or reduced breath sounds in a toddler suggests airway foreign body, even with normal radiographs.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Children <3 years exploring objects orally; nuts, seeds, grapes, hot dogs, toy fragments
Neurologic swallowing impairment, sedation, intoxication, poor dentition in adults

rows.label: Clues
items: Witnessed coughing/gagging during eating or play; symptoms may partially resolve after initial event
★ **Cannot speak, cough effectively, or breathe** → severe airway obstruction
Proximal obstruction: stridor; distal obstruction: focal wheeze, persistent cough, recurrent same-lobe pneumonia
Cyanosis, altered consciousness, exhaustion → imminent respiratory arrest

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Partial ball-valve blockage allows inspiration but limits expiration → distal hyperinflation
Complete bronchial blockage → resorption atelectasis; retained organic material causes inflammation and infection

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Stable child → **chest x-ray**, including expiratory or bilateral decubitus views when feasible
Unilateral air trapping, mediastinal shift, collapse, or radiopaque object may identify location
Most food objects are radiolucent; negative examination/imaging does not exclude a convincing history
★ High suspicion → **bronchoscopy**; avoid delaying definitive evaluation for repeated imaging

rows.label: Tx
items: Effective cough/partial obstruction → encourage coughing, observe closely; no blind finger sweep
★ Infant severe choking: **5 back blows + 5 chest thrusts**, repeat
Age ≥1 year: cycles of five back blows/five abdominal thrusts; pregnancy/marked obesity → chest thrusts
Unresponsive → CPR, inspect mouth during airway opening, remove visible object only
★ Stable retained pediatric object → **rigid bronchoscopy** for retrieval; expert airway team for unstable obstruction

rows.label: Complications
items: Hypoxic brain injury, arrest, postobstructive pneumonia, bronchiectasis, granulation tissue
Removal can cause bleeding, edema, or pneumothorax; persistent symptoms need reassessment

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid small hard foods/toys; cut grapes lengthwise, supervise eating, avoid running with food
Teach caregivers choking response; keep small objects away from young children

rows.label: Mimics
items: Asthma: recurrent diffuse wheeze with bronchodilator response
Croup: preceding URI, barking cough, diffuse upper-airway obstruction
Bronchiolitis: viral prodrome, diffuse crackles/wheezing in an infant

gastric-cancer.name: Gastric cancer
gastric-cancer.scope: Intestinal vs diffuse adenocarcinoma, signet ring cells, linitis plastica, risk factors (H. pylori, ancestry), endoscopy
gastric-cancer.core: Progressive early satiety, weight loss, or upper-GI bleeding warrants gastric malignancy evaluation, particularly with high-risk ancestry or chronic atrophic gastritis.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: H pylori, smoking, salt-preserved foods, pernicious anemia, prior gastric surgery
Higher incidence in East Asian ancestry/immigrants from high-incidence regions; hereditary diffuse disease with CDH1 variants

rows.label: Clues
items: Epigastric discomfort, anorexia, iron-deficiency anemia, vomiting from gastric outlet obstruction
★ **Virchow node**, Sister Mary Joseph nodule or ovarian Krukenberg metastases → advanced disease
Acanthosis nigricans or abrupt multiple seborrheic keratoses may be paraneoplastic

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Intestinal pathway: chronic mucosal injury → atrophy, metaplasia, dysplasia
Diffuse pathway: loss of cellular adhesion → infiltrative wall thickening and poor distensibility

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Upper endoscopy with multiple biopsies**; superficial sampling may miss infiltrative disease
Confirmed malignancy → CT chest/abdomen/pelvis; endoscopic ultrasound for local depth/nodal assessment
Potentially resectable advanced tumor → staging laparoscopy for occult peritoneal disease
Advanced disease → HER2, mismatch-repair/MSI and PD-L1 testing to select systemic treatment

rows.label: Tx
items: Selected superficial mucosal cancers → endoscopic resection
★ Localized resectable cancer → **gastrectomy with lymphadenectomy** and stage-dependent perioperative chemotherapy
Advanced disease → fluoropyrimidine/platinum; biomarker-selected checkpoint inhibitor or HER2-targeted trastuzumab
Obstructing incurable tumor → stent, bypass or feeding access; manage bleeding and nutrition

rows.label: Complications
items: Peritoneal/liver metastases, ascites, hemorrhage; cachexia and obstruction
After gastrectomy → dumping syndrome, iron/B12 deficiency; provide nutritional follow-up

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Eradicate H pylori** and confirm cure; stop smoking, reduce high-salt preserved foods
High-risk families → genetic counseling; targeted endoscopic surveillance rather than universal US screening

rows.label: Mimics
items: Peptic ulcer: benign biopsy; gastric ulcer still requires malignancy exclusion
Gastric MALT lymphoma: lymphoid histology; may regress after H pylori eradication

gastric-cancer.evidence: Not checked online; established clinical teaching.

gastrointestinal-bleeding.name: Gastrointestinal bleeding
gastrointestinal-bleeding.scope: Upper GI bleeding (PUD, varices, Mallory-Weiss), lower GI bleeding (diverticular, angiodysplasia, hemorrhoids), fluid and transfusion thresholds, endoscopy
gastrointestinal-bleeding.core: Hematemesis, melena, or hematochezia → assess hemodynamics before localizing; brisk upper bleeding can present as bright red rectal blood.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: NSAIDs/H pylori → ulcers; cirrhosis → varices; forceful retching → mucosal tear
Anticoagulants/antiplatelets increase severity; older age favors diverticula or angiodysplasia

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Syncope, orthostasis, shock** signal major loss; initial hemoglobin may remain normal
Epigastric pain supports ulcer; painless bleeding favors vascular sources
Recurrent occult loss → iron deficiency
**Melena**, elevated BUN/creatinine ratio → upper source; bilious NG aspirate argues against upper bleeding

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Mucosal injury, portal-pressure collaterals, or fragile vessels rupture into GI lumen
Volume depletion → reduced perfusion; ongoing bleeding may require massive transfusion

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Two large-bore IVs, CBC, type/cross, coagulation tests**, serial hemoglobin; resuscitate before procedures
Upper source → EGD within 24 hours after stabilization; suspected varices → within 12 hours
★ Ongoing hemodynamically significant hematochezia → **CT angiography → embolization** if active extravasation
Stable lower bleeding → bowel preparation and nonemergent colonoscopy; routine <24-hour colonoscopy adds no benefit
Rectal bleeding mixed with stool, age ≥45 → colonoscopy; negative FOBT does not exclude neoplasia

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Crystalloid initially; stable nonischemic adults → **RBC transfusion at hemoglobin <7 g/dL**
Exsanguination or post-crystalloid shock → **RBCs** regardless of hemoglobin, not vasopressors; cardiac ischemia → higher threshold
Severe anticoagulant bleeding → drug-specific reversal; uncontrolled varices → balloon tamponade as temporary bridge only
Failed endoscopy → IR/surgery; massive unlocalized lower bleeding → **total abdominal colectomy**, not segmental
Suspected ulcer → IV PPI; endoscopic hemostasis for active bleeding/visible vessel, then high-dose PPI

rows.label: Complications
items: Rebleeding, aspiration, myocardial ischemia, AKI; variceal bleeding → infection
Massive transfusion → hypocalcemia, hypothermia, coagulopathy; embolization → bowel ischemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Eradicate H pylori and confirm cure; avoid NSAIDs; PPI for high-risk users
After variceal control: nonselective beta-blocker plus repeat banding; recurrent bleeding → TIPS

rows.label: Mimics
items: Iron/bismuth: dark stool without blood loss
Hemoptysis: coughing frothy blood rather than vomiting
Swallowed epistaxis: nasal source on examination

table.title: Source-specific branches
rows: Postretching tear; Boerhaave instead: chest pain, crepitus
Liver trauma + jaundice; blood from ampulla

gastrointestinal-bleeding.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ACG lower GI bleeding 2023](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36735555/), [ACS transfusion guidance 2025](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.11.009).

gender-dysphoria.name: Gender dysphoria
gender-dysphoria.scope: DSM-5 diagnostic criteria, pediatric and adolescent presentations, psychiatric comorbidities, parental support, gender-affirming care, transgender health maintenance
gender-dysphoria.core: Clinically significant distress or functional impairment associated with incongruence between experienced gender and assigned sex.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Rejection, discrimination or forced concealment can amplify distress

rows.label: Clues
items: Children: persistent identity-related wishes and preferences; distress about anatomy
Adolescents: pubertal changes may intensify distress or prompt presentation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Sources of distress vary individually: body characteristics, social recognition, or both

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ DSM-5: symptoms for **≥6 months** plus age-specific criteria
★ Private adolescent interview; screen for depression, anxiety, self-harm, bullying and safety at home

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Support exploration without predetermined outcome; affirm chosen name and pronouns; engage supportive caregivers
Prepubertal: psychosocial support; no endocrine treatment
After puberty begins: specialist assessment for individualized puberty suppression or hormones
Before endocrine treatment: discuss consent, fertility preservation, and expected reversible versus irreversible effects

rows.label: Complications
items: Minority stress and rejection → isolation, school avoidance, suicidality
Endocrine care monitoring: bone accrual during suppression, hematocrit with testosterone, thrombotic risk with estrogen

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Screen based on **organs present**, exposures, age, and risk; offer HPV vaccination and contraception as relevant
Family and school support, anti-bullying measures, connection to affirming mental health care

rows.label: Mimics
items: Gender diversity without distress: no dysphoria diagnosis
Body dysmorphic disorder: perceived appearance flaw rather than gender-related incongruence

table.title: DSM-5 age-specific thresholds
rows: Strong desire or insistence on another gender
Body characteristics, identity, social treatment, feelings

gender-dysphoria.evidence: Checked Endocrine Society gender dysphoria guideline (2017) and guideline resources.

glaucoma.name: Glaucoma
glaucoma.scope: Open-angle glaucoma, acute angle-closure glaucoma, increased intraocular pressure, optic disc cupping, tonometry, visual field testing, topical prostaglandins, laser trabeculoplasty, iridotomy
glaucoma.core: Progressive optic nerve damage threatens vision; a sudden painful red eye from angle closure is an emergency.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Open-angle: older age, family history, African ancestry, myopia, chronic glucocorticoids
Angle closure: shallow chamber, hyperopia, aging lens, pharmacologic dilation

rows.label: Clues
items: Open-angle: central acuity preserved until late
★ Acute closure: halos, vomiting, hazy cornea, **fixed mid-dilated pupil**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Open-angle: trabecular outflow resistance despite patent angle
Pupillary block → bowed iris obstructs trabecular meshwork → rapid IOP rise

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Tonometry** measures IOP; normal pressure does not exclude glaucoma
**Gonioscopy** determines angle anatomy
Disc exam/OCT: increased cup-to-disc ratio, rim thinning, retinal nerve fiber loss
Automated perimetry: nasal step or arcuate scotoma; serial testing tracks progression

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute closure: urgent ophthalmology; acetazolamide plus topical timolol and brimonidine; IV mannitol if refractory
Pilocarpine after IOP falls in pupillary block; delay definitive laser until cornea clears
Open-angle progression despite maximal tolerated therapy → consider filtration surgery

rows.label: Complications
items: Irreversible optic nerve damage and blindness
Latanoprost: iris darkening and eyelash growth

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Prophylactic iridotomy in fellow eye after primary acute closure

rows.label: Mimics
items: Anterior uveitis: small pupil, consensual photophobia, anterior chamber cells
Conjunctivitis: discharge, preserved acuity, minimal pain

glaucoma.evidence: Checked AAO Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma Preferred Practice Pattern (2025).

gonococcal-infection.name: Gonococcal infection
gonococcal-infection.scope: Urethritis/cervicitis, disseminated gonococcal infection, gonococcal arthritis, neonatal conjunctivitis
gonococcal-infection.core: Neisseria gonorrhoeae causes mucosal infection and can disseminate into a dermatitis-tenosynovitis-arthritis syndrome or purulent septic arthritis.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: New/multiple partners, inconsistent barriers, prior STI, younger age
Complement deficiency increases dissemination risk; neonatal exposure during vaginal delivery

rows.label: Clues
items: Dysuria, mucopurulent discharge, friable cervix; rectal/pharyngeal disease often asymptomatic
★ **Migratory arthralgia, tenosynovitis, sparse pustules** → disseminated infection
Neonate: copious purulent conjunctivitis 2–5 days after birth; corneal injury can progress rapidly

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Gram-negative intracellular diplococci adhere to mucosa; antigenic variation permits recurrent infection
Ascending genital spread or bacteremia extends disease beyond initial exposure site

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **NAAT at exposed sites**: urine/vaginal, rectal, pharyngeal; test chlamydia, HIV, syphilis
Symptomatic male urethral Gram stain may show intracellular diplococci; less reliable at other sites
Dissemination: blood/synovial cultures and mucosal NAAT; negative joint culture does not exclude diagnosis
Suspected treatment failure → culture and antimicrobial susceptibility, assess reinfection

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Uncomplicated: **ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once**; ≥150 kg → 1 g once
Chlamydia not excluded → doxycycline 7 days, don't await results; pregnancy, older exam questions → azithromycin
★ Disseminated disease → **IV/IM ceftriaxone**, hospitalization initially; drain purulent joint
Neonatal infection → systemic ceftriaxone, or cefotaxime if bilirubin/calcium concerns; topical treatment alone insufficient

rows.label: Complications
items: PID, infertility, ectopic pregnancy, epididymitis, corneal perforation
Rare endocarditis/meningitis; untreated septic arthritis damages cartilage

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Treat partners from preceding **60 days**; abstain 7 days after treatment and until partners treated
Retest at 3 months; pharyngeal test-of-cure at 7–14 days; routine urogenital test-of-cure unnecessary
Condoms, risk-based screening; neonatal erythromycin eye ointment prevents gonococcal ophthalmia

rows.label: Mimics
items: Chlamydia: similar urethritis/cervicitis, NAAT distinguishes
Reactive arthritis: sterile arthritis after infection, conjunctivitis/enthesitis
Staphylococcal arthritis: usually isolated hot joint without migratory skin-tendon syndrome

gout.name: Gout and crystal arthropathy
gout.scope: Acute gout, chronic gout and urate lowering, pseudogout (CPPD)
gout.core: Abrupt intensely painful inflammatory arthritis from crystal deposition; gout and CPPD require different long-term prevention despite similar flare management.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Gout: CKD, obesity, alcohol, purines/fructose, thiazide/loop diuretics, low-dose aspirin
CPPD: older age, joint injury, hyperparathyroidism, hemochromatosis, hypomagnesemia
Flares follow surgery, dehydration, illness, or changes in urate concentration

rows.label: Clues
