rows: Unanticipated death/serious harm/life-saving rescue; prompts RCA
Upstream scheduling/staffing flaw; fix system, not individual

medical-errors-and-patient-safety.evidence: Not checked online; established patient-safety terminology and ethical disclosure principles.

menopause.name: Menopause
menopause.scope: Perimenopause, menopause transition, vasomotor symptoms, genitourinary syndrome of menopause, HRT
menopause.core: Menopause is 12 months without menses from ovarian follicle depletion; manage bothersome symptoms according to uterine status and hormone-treatment risk.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Natural transition typically in late 40s–50s; smoking, oophorectomy, chemotherapy or pelvic radiation accelerate onset
Menopause before 40 suggests primary ovarian insufficiency and requires a separate evaluation

rows.label: Clues
items: Perimenopause: variable cycles, skipped periods, fertility remains; isolated irregularity → **reassurance**, no biopsy
Vasomotor episodes: abrupt heat, flushing, sweating, disturbed sleep; mood symptoms can coexist
Genitourinary syndrome: dryness, dyspareunia, urinary urgency and recurrent UTIs; pale thin friable mucosa
Urogenital estrogen loss: **negative cultures**, possible sterile pyuria; friable mucosa → spotting, postcoital bleeding

rows.label: Pathophys
items: ↓Follicles → ↓estradiol/inhibin and ↑FSH; hypothalamic thermoregulatory changes drive hot flashes
Urogenital estrogen deficiency thins epithelium, raises vaginal pH and changes flora

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical symptoms at **≥45 years → clinical diagnosis**; routine FSH unnecessary
Unexpected amenorrhea → pregnancy test; earlier menopause → FSH/estradiol and targeted thyroid/prolactin evaluation
Postmenopausal bleeding → endometrial evaluation; do not attribute to normal transition
Hormonal contraception alters bleeding/FSH interpretation; amenorrhea on contraception alone does not establish menopause

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Bothersome hot flashes, low risk, generally <60 or within 10 years → **systemic estrogen**
★ Intact uterus → **add progestogen**; hysterectomy → estrogen alone usually sufficient
Avoid systemic hormones with unexplained bleeding, estrogen-sensitive cancer, prior VTE/stroke/MI or active liver disease
Hormones unsuitable → **venlafaxine, paroxetine or gabapentin**; selected fezolinetant requires liver monitoring
★ Isolated GSM → lubricants/moisturizers then **low-dose vaginal estrogen**; routine progestogen generally unnecessary

rows.label: Complications
items: Bone loss, fracture, sexual dysfunction; oral systemic estrogen increases VTE/stroke risk
Combined systemic hormones can increase breast cancer risk; unopposed uterine estrogen causes endometrial hyperplasia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Weight-bearing exercise, adequate calcium/vitamin D, smoking cessation; age/risk-based osteoporosis screening
Hormone treatment not for primary cardiovascular/dementia prevention; reassess symptoms and risks periodically
Continue contraception during transition until menopause criteria met; menopausal hormones do not prevent pregnancy

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hyperthyroidism: persistent heat intolerance, tachycardia, suppressed TSH
Pregnancy: positive hCG despite irregular cycles

microcytic-anemia.name: Microcytic anemia
microcytic-anemia.scope: Iron deficiency, anemia of chronic disease, thalassemia, sideroblastic anemia
microcytic-anemia.core: Low hemoglobin with MCV <80 fL: distinguish depleted iron, inflammatory iron sequestration, globin underproduction, and defective heme synthesis.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Menstrual/GI blood loss, pregnancy, low intake, malabsorption → iron depletion
Chronic infection, autoimmune disease, malignancy → inflammatory anemia
Inherited hemoglobin disorders; alcohol, lead, isoniazid, myelodysplasia → disordered heme production
Preterm birth → low stores, screen toddlers; infant microcytosis → **dietary history** for excess cow's milk

rows.label: Clues
items: Fatigue, pallor, exertional dyspnea; severe anemia → tachycardia, angina, syncope
Pica, koilonychia, restless legs suggest iron deficiency
Markedly low MCV, preserved hemoglobin, high RBC count, **normal RDW** (Mentzer <13) suggest thalassemia trait

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Inflammation → ↑hepcidin → ferroportin suppression, impaired absorption and iron release; cytokines blunt **erythropoietin**
Sideroblasts: mitochondrial iron accumulation in erythroblasts from impaired protoporphyrin synthesis

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CBC/smear → ferritin**, iron, TIBC, transferrin saturation; ferritin rises with inflammation
★ Ferritin **<45 ng/mL in anemia** supports iron deficiency; normal result cannot exclude during inflammation
★ Adult men/postmenopausal women with iron deficiency → **EGD + colonoscopy**; consider celiac testing
Hemoglobin electrophoresis for suspected beta-thalassemia; alpha trait may require genetic testing; exposure → blood lead
Microcytosis + afebrile pain crisis, at-risk ancestry → **smear** for sickled cells (sickle–β-thalassemia)

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Iron deficiency → **oral ferrous sulfate**; intolerance/malabsorption or rapid replacement need → IV iron
Treat bleeding source; continue iron about 3 months beyond hemoglobin normalization; reassess nonresponse
Inflammatory anemia → treat underlying disease; selected CKD → iron ± erythropoietin
Sideroblastic: remove trigger, pyridoxine if isoniazid-related; severe thalassemia → transfusion/chelation

rows.label: Complications
items: Iron deficiency: developmental effects in children, adverse pregnancy outcomes
Repeated transfusion → iron overload, cardiac/hepatic injury; oral iron → constipation, dark stool
Four-gene α-deletion → **Hb Barts** (γ4) → severe fetal anemia, hydrops fetalis

rows.label: Prevention
items: Adequate dietary iron, pregnancy supplementation, lead-exposure reduction
★ **No empiric long-term iron for thalassemia trait** without documented deficiency

rows.label: Mimics
items: Acute blood loss: initially normocytic; hemoglobin may lag volume loss
Hemolysis: reticulocytosis, ↑LDH/indirect bilirubin, ↓haptoglobin

microcytic-anemia.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [AGA iron deficiency evaluation 2020](https://gastro.org/clinical-guidance/gastrointestinal-evaluation-of-iron-deficiency-anemia/); remaining hematology established teaching.

multiple-gestation.name: Multiple gestation
multiple-gestation.scope: Dichorionic diamniotic (lambda sign), monochorionic diamniotic (T-sign), monochorionic monoamniotic, twin-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS), selective FGR, delivery timing recommendations
multiple-gestation.core: Chorionicity and amnionicity determine twin-specific surveillance, complications, and delivery timing; establish both on first-trimester ultrasound.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Dizygotic twins: ovulation induction/assisted reproduction, maternal age, family history
Monozygotic splitting timing determines placental and sac sharing

rows.label: Clues
items: Uterus larger than dates, exaggerated pregnancy symptoms; ultrasound confirms fetal number
★ Shared placenta with **oligohydramnios/polyhydramnios sequence** → TTTS; small/absent donor bladder
Selective FGR: one small twin, discordant estimated weights; assess each umbilical artery Doppler

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Placental vascular anastomoses permit imbalanced flow in monochorionic twins
Donor hypovolemia reduces urine; recipient hypervolemia increases urine and cardiac strain

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **First-trimester ultrasound** identifies shared placenta and intertwin membrane
Monochorionic diamniotic → ultrasound **every 2 weeks from 16 weeks** for fluid/bladders
Serial growth in all twins; Doppler and more frequent assessment when growth discordance develops
TTTS donor deepest pocket ≤2 cm, recipient ≥8 cm; staging incorporates bladder, Doppler, hydrops

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ TTTS stages II–IV at 16–26 weeks → **fetoscopic laser ablation** of placental anastomoses
Asymptomatic stage I → at least weekly surveillance; refer fetal intervention center if progression/symptoms
★ Diamniotic twins with **first twin cephalic** may deliver vaginally with experienced team
Monoamniotic twins → cesarean; fetal deterioration, preeclampsia, or severe growth issues may require earlier delivery

rows.label: Complications
items: Preterm birth, preeclampsia, anemia, gestational diabetes, postpartum hemorrhage
Monoamniotic cord entanglement; monochorionic co-twin death can cause surviving twin neurologic injury

rows.label: Prevention
items: Low-dose aspirin for preeclampsia prevention; optimize iron/nutrition; single-embryo transfer reduces iatrogenic multiples

rows.label: Mimics
items: Incorrect dates/macrosomia: enlarged uterus but singleton on imaging
Twin anemia-polycythemia sequence: discordant MCA velocities without major fluid imbalance

multiple-myeloma.name: Multiple myeloma
multiple-myeloma.scope: CRAB features (hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, anemia, bone lytic lesions), SPEP/UPEP M-spike, serum free light chains, bone marrow biopsy (>10% plasma cells), MGUS, smoldering myeloma
multiple-myeloma.core: A clonal plasma-cell malignancy causes monoclonal protein production and organ damage; modern biomarkers can establish treatment-requiring disease before symptoms.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older age, Black ancestry, male sex, preexisting MGUS; usually no identifiable preventable exposure

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **CRAB**: hypercalcemia, renal impairment, anemia, lytic bone lesions
Back/rib pain, pathologic fracture, recurrent bacterial infection, high total protein, rouleaux
Acute weakness/back pain → cord compression; proteinuria or restrictive cardiomyopathy → consider AL amyloid

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Marrow expansion suppresses blood formation; osteoclast activation without osteoblast response causes bone destruction
Light chains injure renal tubules; low polyclonal immunoglobulins → **encapsulated bacteria**, e.g., pneumococcus

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **SPEP/immunofixation + free light chains**, urine studies; light-chain disease may lack serum spike
★ **Bone marrow biopsy** quantifies clonal plasma cells; whole-body low-dose CT/MRI assesses bone disease
Active disease: ≥10% clonal marrow cells/plasmacytoma plus attributable CRAB or myeloma-defining biomarker
SLiM: marrow ≥60%; involved/uninvolved FLC ratio ≥100 with involved FLC ≥100 mg/L
MRI >1 focal lesion ≥5 mm defines active disease; bone scan may miss lytic lesions

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Bortezomib-based combination** ± daratumumab/lenalidomide/dexamethasone; selected patients → autologous transplant
Hypercalcemia → saline plus antiresorptive; AKI → hydration, avoid NSAIDs/contrast and rapidly reduce light chains
Cord compression → dexamethasone and urgent MRI/radiation or surgery; treat infections promptly
MGUS/smoldering disease generally monitored; high-risk smoldering disease merits specialist assessment

rows.label: Complications
items: Cast nephropathy, vertebral collapse, hyperviscosity, AL amyloidosis; treatment-related neuropathy, infections and thrombosis
Urine dipstick detects albumin, misses light chains; negative dipstick does not exclude cast nephropathy

rows.label: Prevention
items: Vaccines, bisphosphonates; proteasome inhibitors → antiviral prophylaxis; immunomodulators → thromboprophylaxis by risk

rows.label: Mimics
items: Metastatic carcinoma: destructive lesions without clonal plasma-cell findings
Waldenström macroglobulinemia: IgM, hyperviscosity/lymphadenopathy, usually no lytic lesions

multiple-myeloma.evidence: Criteria checked 2026-10-30: [IMWG diagnostic criteria](https://www.myeloma.org/newly-diagnosed/multiple-myeloma-diagnostic-criteria); treatment: established generalist teaching.

multiple-sclerosis.name: Multiple sclerosis
multiple-sclerosis.scope: Relapsing-remitting, optic neuritis, transverse myelitis, internuclear ophthalmoplegia (MLF lesion), Uhthoff phenomenon, Lhermitte sign, disease-modifying therapies
multiple-sclerosis.core: Neurologic deficits separated in location and time, often including optic neuritis, suggest inflammatory CNS demyelination.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Young adulthood, female sex, **Northern European ancestry**, family history; EBV, smoking, low vitamin D

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Optic neuritis: **pain with eye movement**, monocular loss, poor color vision, afferent pupillary defect, often normal fundus
Internuclear ophthalmoplegia: **MLF lesion**, impaired ipsilateral adduction, contralateral abducting nystagmus; convergence intact
Uhthoff: old deficits worsen with heat; Lhermitte: neck flexion triggers electric spinal sensation
Transverse myelitis: weakness, sensory level, urinary dysfunction; acute relapse generally lasts >24 hours

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Immune-mediated oligodendrocyte/myelin injury → CNS plaques, conduction block and eventual axonal loss
Relapsing-remitting: attacks with recovery; progressive forms: accumulating disability between or without attacks

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **MRI brain/cord**: periventricular, cortical/juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal lesions; 2024 criteria add optic nerve
Classic time dissemination: new follow-up lesion or simultaneous enhancing/nonenhancing lesions; exclude better explanation
CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands support diagnosis; revised criteria also accept kappa free-light-chain index
Atypical severe visual loss/long cord lesion → serum AQP4/MOG antibodies; revised criteria permit selected earlier diagnoses
Suspected relapse → exclude fever, UTI and metabolic triggers before escalating immunosuppression

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Disabling relapse/optic neuritis → **high-dose IV methylprednisolone**, not low-dose prednisone; refractory → plasma exchange
★ Relapsing disease → early disease-modifying drug, e.g., **ocrelizumab**, tailored to activity and pregnancy plans
Lower-activity options include interferon-beta or glatiramer; natalizumab requires JC-virus/PML risk assessment
Baclofen for spasticity; rehabilitation, bladder care and treatment of neuropathic pain
Isolated heat/infection-related worsening → treat trigger; not automatically a new inflammatory attack

rows.label: Complications
items: Gait impairment, falls, neurogenic bladder, depression and cognitive dysfunction
Immunosuppressive treatment → infection; some agents carry PML risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation, exercise, vaccination; review contraception/pregnancy before disease-modifying drugs

rows.label: Mimics
items: B12 deficiency: symmetric posterior-column dysfunction, macrocytosis
NMOSD: AQP4-positive, often severe attacks; some MS drugs worsen disease
Stroke: abrupt maximal deficit, vascular territory

muscular-dystrophies.name: Muscular dystrophies
muscular-dystrophies.scope: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (dystrophin frameshift, Gowers sign, dilated cardiomyopathy), Becker muscular dystrophy, myotonic dystrophy (CTG repeat, myotonia, cataracts, balding), genetic testing
muscular-dystrophies.core: Progressive inherited muscle weakness: childhood pelvic-girdle weakness suggests dystrophinopathy; delayed relaxation with multisystem disease suggests myotonic dystrophy.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Duchenne/Becker: X-linked recessive; affected boys, maternal carrier relatives; de novo variants common
Myotonic dystrophy type 1: autosomal dominant with anticipation; severe congenital disease often maternally transmitted

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Gowers maneuver** and calf pseudohypertrophy indicate proximal weakness
Dystrophinopathy: waddling gait, delayed motor milestones; preserved sensation
Grip/percussion myotonia: delayed muscle relaxation, often improving with repeated movement

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Dystrophin deficiency destabilizes muscle membrane → myofiber necrosis and fat/fibrous replacement
Myotonic dystrophy: toxic expanded-repeat RNA disrupts splicing in multiple tissues

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CK → genetic testing**; dystrophin deletion/duplication analysis, then sequencing if needed
Myotonic phenotype → DMPK repeat-expansion testing; muscle biopsy rarely needed
ECG/echocardiography and pulmonary function at diagnosis and serially; assess swallowing and sleep ventilation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Duchenne: **prednisone or deflazacort**, stretching, mobility support; specialist genotype-directed options
Cardiomyopathy → ACE inhibitor/ARB, add beta-blocker; respiratory weakness → assisted cough/noninvasive ventilation
Disabling myotonia → mexiletine after cardiac evaluation; high-grade conduction block → pacemaker
Avoid succinylcholine; dystrophinopathy also carries rhabdomyolysis risk with volatile anesthetics

rows.label: Complications
items: Dilated cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias, restrictive respiratory failure, aspiration, scoliosis, contractures
Steroid-associated osteoporosis and adrenal suppression; myotonic dystrophy → sudden cardiac death

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Carrier testing and genetic counseling**; screen female dystrophin carriers for cardiomyopathy
Vaccination, nutritional support, bone health monitoring, regular cardiac/respiratory surveillance

rows.label: Mimics
items: SMA: areflexia, fasciculations, relatively modest CK elevation
Inflammatory myopathy: acquired weakness, inflammation; no characteristic inheritance pattern

table.title: Distinguishing types
rows: Distal weakness, cataracts, frontal balding, testicular atrophy

muscular-dystrophies.evidence: Not checked online; established phenotypes and supportive treatment; novel genotype-specific treatments omitted.

myocarditis.name: Myocarditis
myocarditis.scope: Viral myocarditis, postviral heart failure, elevated cardiac biomarkers, ECG changes, cardiac MRI, supportive heart failure therapy
myocarditis.core: New chest pain, arrhythmia or heart failure after a viral syndrome raises concern for inflammatory myocardial injury.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Recent viral illness, autoimmune disease, immune checkpoint inhibitors and selected drug hypersensitivity
Chagas exposure and giant-cell/eosinophilic disorders matter in selected epidemiologic or fulminant presentations

rows.label: Clues
items: Fatigue, dyspnea, chest discomfort, palpitations; tachycardia disproportionate to fever
Troponin elevation, nonspecific ST–T abnormalities, ventricular ectopy; normal initial studies do not exclude
★ Syncope, sustained ventricular arrhythmia, high-grade AV block or shock → **high-risk myocarditis**
Concurrent pericarditis may produce pleuritic positional pain and diffuse ST elevation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Direct injury and immune-mediated inflammation damage cardiomyocytes → edema, necrosis and ventricular dysfunction
Residual scar creates an arrhythmic substrate even when systolic function improves

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ ECG, troponin, BNP and **echocardiography** assess injury, rhythm and function
★ **Cardiac MRI** identifies edema and nonischemic late gadolinium enhancement
Exclude ACS with coronary assessment when presentation/risk warrants; troponin alone cannot distinguish
Endomyocardial biopsy for selected fulminant, arrhythmic or unexplained progressive disease when etiology changes treatment
Routine broad viral serology rarely establishes myocardial cause

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Stable systolic HF → **diuresis and guideline-directed HF drugs**; defer beta blocker during shock
Hemodynamic compromise → ICU, vasopressors/inotropes and temporary mechanical circulatory support when refractory
Treat arrhythmias/AV block; pacing or defibrillation support when necessary
No routine steroids for presumed viral disease; giant-cell, eosinophilic and immune-mediated forms may need immunosuppression
Avoid NSAIDs for isolated myocarditis with HF; pericarditic pain requires individualized assessment

rows.label: Complications
items: Dilated cardiomyopathy, persistent HF, ventricular tachycardia, sudden death and intracardiac thrombosis

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Restrict strenuous exercise during active inflammation; return after symptom, imaging and rhythm reassessment
Classic restriction 3–6 months; newer guidance allows earlier individualized return in selected fully recovered athletes
Follow-up echo/MRI, ambulatory ECG and exercise testing guide clearance

rows.label: Mimics
items: MI: coronary distribution ischemia/scar and culprit artery
Stress cardiomyopathy: characteristic reversible wall-motion pattern
Pericarditis alone: pericardial inflammation without myocardial dysfunction

narcolepsy.name: Narcolepsy
narcolepsy.scope: Excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, hypnagogic and hypnopompic hallucinations, sleep paralysis, polysomnography and MSLT, hypocretin (orexin) deficiency, modafinil, sodium oxybate
narcolepsy.core: Irresistible sleep attacks despite sufficient nighttime sleep, with emotion-triggered loss of muscle tone strongly suggesting type 1 narcolepsy.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Usually adolescent/young-adult onset; genetic susceptibility with probable autoimmune hypothalamic neuron loss

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Cataplexy**: seconds to minutes of weakness, preserved consciousness; laughter or surprise trigger
Vivid hallucinations at sleep onset or awakening; transient inability to move at sleep transitions
Short naps refreshing; disrupted nighttime sleep; daytime automatic behaviors

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Type 1: deficient hypothalamic hypocretin/orexin → unstable wakefulness and REM intrusion
Type 2: no cataplexy, no demonstrated orexin deficiency

rows.label: Dx
items: Daily sleepiness ≥3 months; sleep diary/actigraphy first to document sufficient sleep
★ Overnight **polysomnography → next-day MSLT**; exclude untreated OSA and sleep deprivation
Mean sleep latency ≤8 minutes plus ≥2 sleep-onset REM periods; preceding PSG can contribute one
Low CSF hypocretin supports type 1; usually unnecessary with characteristic cataplexy and diagnostic testing
Coordinate stimulant/REM-suppressing drug washout before testing; abrupt withdrawal can confound results

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Daytime sleepiness → **modafinil**; alternatives methylphenidate, pitolisant, solriamfetol
★ Prominent cataplexy → **sodium oxybate**; venlafaxine can suppress attacks
Oxybate: avoid alcohol, opioids, benzodiazepines because of respiratory/CNS depression
Scheduled naps, regular nighttime sleep, workplace/school accommodations

rows.label: Complications
items: Motor vehicle crashes, impaired school/work performance, depression
Modafinil reduces hormonal contraceptive effectiveness; review pregnancy planning

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid driving or hazardous work until sleepiness controlled; reassess driving safety during follow-up

rows.label: Mimics
items: OSA: snoring, witnessed apneas, abnormal respiratory PSG
Idiopathic hypersomnia: long unrefreshing sleep, fewer sleep-onset REM periods
Syncope/seizure: loss of consciousness or postictal confusion rather than isolated cataplexy

neonatal-respiratory-distress.name: Neonatal respiratory distress
neonatal-respiratory-distress.scope: Transient tachypnea of the newborn, respiratory distress syndrome, meconium aspiration syndrome, persistent PH
neonatal-respiratory-distress.core: Tachypnea, retractions, grunting, or cyanosis after birth requires stabilization while gestational age, delivery history, and imaging narrow the cause.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prematurity/maternal diabetes → RDS; cesarean without labor → TTN; post-term/meconium → aspiration
Maternal fever, prolonged membrane rupture or inadequate GBS prophylaxis raise concern for infectious pneumonia

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Apnea, bradycardia, poor perfusion or severe hypoxemia** → immediate neonatal resuscitation
PPHN: labile hypoxemia, preductal right-hand saturation higher than postductal foot saturation
Unilateral absent breath sounds or abrupt deterioration → pneumothorax; scaphoid abdomen → diaphragmatic hernia
TTN improves within 24–72 hours; persistent/worsening disease warrants reassessment

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Poor lung expansion, airway obstruction or V/Q mismatch impairs oxygenation
PPHN: persistently high pulmonary resistance causes right-to-left ductal/atrial shunting

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Pulse oximetry, blood gas and chest radiograph** after initial stabilization
Pre/postductal saturation comparison and echocardiography for suspected PPHN; exclude structural heart disease
Possible infection → blood culture and CBC; biomarkers cannot independently exclude sepsis
Persistent unexplained hypoxemia → echocardiography rather than assuming primary pulmonary disease

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Warmth, oxygen titrated to neonatal targets; **CPAP** for breathing infant with distress
Apnea/gasping or HR <100 → positive-pressure ventilation; ineffective ventilation requires corrective steps/advanced airway
RDS with increasing oxygen need → intratracheal surfactant; mechanical ventilation if noninvasive support fails
★ PPHN → lung recruitment/oxygenation, **inhaled nitric oxide** for suitable term/near-term infants; refractory → ECMO
Meconium: no routine tracheal suction; suction only obstructed ventilation; suspected sepsis → ampicillin/gentamicin

rows.label: Complications
items: Air leak, hypoxic brain injury, death; prematurity/ventilation → bronchopulmonary dysplasia, retinopathy

rows.label: Prevention
items: Antenatal corticosteroids when preterm delivery expected; avoid elective delivery before 39 weeks
Treat maternal infection, provide indicated intrapartum GBS prophylaxis

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cyanotic congenital heart disease: abnormal cardiac anatomy on echo
Congenital diaphragmatic hernia: bowel in chest; intubate and decompress stomach, avoid bag-mask ventilation

table.title: Lung patterns
rows: Low volumes, diffuse ground glass/air bronchograms
May be normal or reflect trigger

neurocutaneous-disorders.name: Neurocutaneous disorders
neurocutaneous-disorders.scope: Neurofibromatosis type 1, neurofibromatosis type 2, tuberous sclerosis, Sturge-Weber syndrome, von Hippel-Lindau disease, ataxia-telangiectasia
neurocutaneous-disorders.core: Characteristic skin or ocular lesions plus neurologic tumors, seizures, or progressive ataxia suggest an inherited or mosaic multisystem disorder.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: NF1, NF2-related schwannomatosis, TSC, VHL: autosomal dominant; frequent de novo variants
Ataxia-telangiectasia: autosomal recessive; Sturge-Weber: sporadic somatic mosaicism

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Changing painful neurofibroma**, rapid growth, or new weakness → malignant transformation concern
Early focal seizures or developmental regression → evaluate structural cerebral lesions
NF2: hearing loss/tinnitus; NF1: cutaneous neurofibromas and childhood learning difficulties

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Tumor suppressor dysfunction → hamartomas or neoplasms; ATM defect → impaired DNA repair

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical pattern + genetic testing**; targeted MRI for neurologic or tumor symptoms
NF1: ≥2 criteria; ≥6 café-au-lait macules, size >5 mm prepubertal, >15 mm postpubertal
TSC: two major features or one major plus two minor; pathogenic variant also diagnostic

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptomatic tumors → specialist resection; TSC growing lesions → **everolimus** in selected cases
TSC infantile spasms → vigabatrin; other seizures → antiseizure drugs
Sturge-Weber seizures → levetiracetam; refractory focal epilepsy → surgical evaluation
Ataxia-telangiectasia: rehabilitation, infection treatment; minimize ionizing radiation

rows.label: Complications
items: NF1: malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor; VHL: renal carcinoma and pheochromocytoma
TSC: hydrocephalus, renal hemorrhage; ataxia-telangiectasia: lymphoma/leukemia, recurrent sinopulmonary infections

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Genetic counseling**; syndrome-specific eye, hearing, renal, and tumor surveillance
Sturge-Weber: ophthalmology follow-up for glaucoma; NF1: childhood BP and vision monitoring

rows.label: Mimics
items: Isolated café-au-lait macules: no additional diagnostic criteria
Friedreich ataxia: areflexia, cardiomyopathy, no ocular telangiectasias

table.title: Signature findings
rows: Axillary freckling, Lisch nodules, optic glioma
Ash-leaf macules, angiofibromas, cortical tubers, renal angiomyolipomas

neurocutaneous-disorders.evidence: Not checked online; established clinical genetics teaching.

nonsteroidal-anti-inflammatory-drugs.name: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
nonsteroidal-anti-inflammatory-drugs.scope: COX-1 and COX-2 inhibition mechanism, renal adverse effects (sodium retention, acute kidney injury), gastrointestinal toxicity, cardiovascular risks
nonsteroidal-anti-inflammatory-drugs.core: NSAIDs reduce pain, inflammation, and fever through cyclooxygenase inhibition, with gastrointestinal, renal, and cardiovascular tradeoffs.

rows.label: Use
items: ★ Pain, dysmenorrhea, renal colic, gout; **lowest effective dose, shortest duration**
Topical diclofenac for localized joint pain reduces systemic exposure

rows.label: Mechanism
items: COX-1: gastric/platelet/renal effects; COX-2: inflammatory prostaglandins and endothelial prostacyclin
Most reversibly inhibit enzymes; aspirin irreversibly acetylates platelet COX-1

rows.label: Adverse
items: ★ ↓Prostaglandin/prostacyclin → **afferent arteriolar constriction** → AKI, hyperkalemia, sodium retention, hypertension/HF worsening
★ Gastritis, **ulcer/bleeding**; platelet inhibition except with selective COX-2 agents
MI/stroke; interstitial nephritis, analgesic nephropathy (chronic daily use, papillary necrosis); bronchospasm in aspirin-sensitive asthma

rows.label: Avoid
items: Active GI bleeding, severe CKD, decompensated HF, peri-CABG setting
Pregnancy ≥20 weeks generally avoid; later gestation → ductal closure and fetal renal injury
Aspirin in children with viral illness → Reye syndrome

rows.label: Interactions
items: ★ ACE inhibitor/ARB + diuretic + NSAID → **high AKI risk**
Anticoagulants/antiplatelets → bleeding; NSAIDs can increase lithium and methotrexate exposure

rows.label: Monitor
items: BP, edema, creatinine, K; assess melena/anemia and prior ulcer history
High GI risk → consider PPI; reassess need rather than automatically continuing indefinitely
Rising creatinine or BP → stop NSAID, switch to **acetaminophen**

rows.label: Traps
items: Celecoxib reduces GI/platelet effects but retains renal and thrombotic risks
Prescribed low-dose aspirin for obstetric indications remains an exception to pregnancy NSAID restriction
Do not combine multiple NSAIDs for additional analgesia

nonsteroidal-anti-inflammatory-drugs.evidence: Pregnancy safety checked 2026-10-30: [FDA NSAID warning](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-safety-and-availability/fda-recommends-avoiding-use-nsaids-pregnancy-20-weeks-or-later-because-they-can-result-low-amniotic); other pharmacology: established teaching.

opioid-prescribing-and-safety.name: Opioid prescribing and safety
opioid-prescribing-and-safety.scope: Chronic opioid therapy, prescription drug monitoring, opioid tapering, misuse risk assessment, managing refill requests, naloxone co-prescribing
opioid-prescribing-and-safety.core: Use opioids only when expected functional benefit exceeds harm, with shared goals, ongoing reassessment, and a plan for safer prescribing.

rows.label: Principle
items: Chronic pain: prefer nonopioid options; individualize benefit–harm assessment without rigid dose ceilings
CDC outpatient guideline excludes sickle-cell pain, cancer treatment, palliative and end-of-life care

rows.label: Do
items: ★ Before starting: **PDMP, substance-use/mental-health review**, functional goals, risk discussion
Immediate-release, lowest effective dose; reassess at 1–4 weeks after starting/escalating, then regularly
★ **Offer naloxone**: overdose risk with prior overdose, OUD, apnea, benzodiazepines, higher doses

rows.label: Don't
items: Avoid opioid–benzodiazepine combinations when possible; discuss alcohol and driving impairment
Never dismiss/prescribe solely from risk score, urine result, or early refill request

rows.label: Exceptions
items: ★ Refill concern → **nonjudgmental review**, PDMP, call prescriber; assess withdrawal, pain, misuse
Harms exceed benefits → collaborative taper; imminent overdose danger → urgent intervention
Opioid-use disorder → offer buprenorphine/methadone; continue pain care and arrange treatment support

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **No abrupt forced discontinuation**; individualized taper may take months/years
Toxicology testing supports safety, not punishment; confirm unexpected findings and assay limitations
Physical dependence/tolerance alone during supervised treatment does not establish opioid-use disorder

opioid-toxicity.name: Opioid toxicity
opioid-toxicity.scope: Opioid toxidrome, naloxone administration and titration, observation period, precipitated withdrawal
opioid-toxicity.core: Depressed consciousness, slow breathing, and pinpoint pupils after opioid exposure; ventilation takes priority over full awakening.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Fentanyl or heroin exposure, dose escalation, renal dysfunction, long-acting opioids
Alcohol/benzodiazepine co-ingestion; lost tolerance after detoxification, hospitalization, or incarceration

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Bradypnea or apnea** with hypoxemia; reduced bowel sounds, bradycardia, hypotension
Miosis may be absent with severe hypoxia or co-ingestion; needle marks are not required
Pulmonary edema, aspiration, hypothermia, prolonged immobilization may accompany overdose
Chronic use: daytime sleepiness, constipation, apathy, falling grades, miosis, slow breathing

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Mu-receptor activation suppresses medullary ventilatory response to CO2
Naloxone competitively reverses opioid effects but often wears off before the causative opioid

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis**; bedside glucose, pulse oximetry, capnography; do not await toxicology
Urine opiate immunoassay detects morphine/heroin/codeine; may miss fentanyl, methadone, and oxycodone
ECG for methadone-associated QT prolongation; acetaminophen level with uncertain combination-product ingestion

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Open airway, **bag-mask ventilation**, oxygen; intubate if ventilation cannot be maintained
★ **Naloxone** IV titrated to adequate breathing; intranasal/IM route if IV unavailable
Dependent but breathing: start low; apnea/no response: prompt larger/repeated doses, especially fentanyl analogs
Repeated recurrence → naloxone infusion; coma despite repeated doses → evaluate additional causes
Short-acting reversal: observe ≥4 hours after last naloxone; long-acting/recurrent sedation → prolonged monitoring/admission

rows.label: Complications
items: Anoxic brain injury, aspiration pneumonia, rhabdomyolysis, compartment syndrome
Precipitated withdrawal: agitation, vomiting, diarrhea, tachycardia; rare pulmonary edema after reversal

rows.label: Prevention
items: Take-home naloxone, overdose-response training, avoid sedative combinations; offer buprenorphine and addiction follow-up

rows.label: Mimics
items: Pontine hemorrhage: focal neurologic findings, no meaningful naloxone response
Clonidine poisoning: marked bradycardia with similar pupils
Sedative overdose: usually normal pupils; incomplete naloxone response

osteoarthritis.name: Osteoarthritis
osteoarthritis.scope: Clinical diagnosis (Heberden/Bouchard nodes, activity-related pain), radiographic findings, nonpharmacologic therapy, oral and topical NSAIDs, injections
osteoarthritis.core: Activity-related joint pain with brief morning stiffness, crepitus and bony enlargement suggests degenerative joint disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older age, **obesity** (strongest modifiable), prior trauma, malalignment, repetitive occupational loading
Family history, particularly hand disease; obesity affects both mechanical and metabolic risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Morning stiffness generally **<30 minutes**; pain improves with rest early in disease
Knees, hips, first carpometacarpal, DIP and PIP commonly involved; MCP usually spared
Heberden nodes: DIP; Bouchard nodes: PIP; reduced motion and varus/valgus deformity
Hip disease: groin pain with restricted internal rotation; referred pain can localize to knee

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Articular cartilage loss, subchondral remodeling and osteophytes; low-grade synovial inflammation
Joint pain arises from innervated surrounding structures rather than aneural cartilage itself

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical presentation → **clinical diagnosis**; imaging unnecessary for straightforward mild disease
Weight-bearing radiographs if uncertain, severe or worsening: asymmetric joint-space narrowing, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis/cysts
★ Hot acutely swollen joint → **arthrocentesis**; not an OA flare; mild cool effusion → x-ray, simple analgesic
OA fluid noninflammatory: usually WBC <2000/µL; inflammatory markers generally normal

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ First-line **exercise, strengthening, weight loss**; cane contralateral to painful hip/knee
★ Knee/hand pain → **topical diclofenac**; oral NSAID if insufficient and renal/GI/CV risks acceptable
Acetaminophen if unable to use NSAIDs (older exam questions may expect it first); duloxetine for persistent pain
Intra-articular glucocorticoid for short-term relief; avoid routine opioids and hyaluronic acid injections
Severe pain/function loss despite conservative treatment → **joint replacement**

rows.label: Complications
items: Functional limitation, falls, reduced activity and secondary deconditioning
NSAIDs → GI bleeding, AKI, fluid retention; arthroplasty → infection or VTE

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Weight loss** best prevents knee OA, beyond exercise alone; conditioning, injury prevention; no complete joint rest

rows.label: Mimics
items: Rheumatoid arthritis: prolonged stiffness, boggy symmetric MCP/wrist synovitis, marginal erosions, DIP spared
CPPD: acute inflammatory flares, chondrocalcinosis
Septic arthritis: fever, severe painful passive motion, positive synovial culture
Trochanteric bursitis: lateral hip pain over greater trochanter, not groin pain

osteoarthritis.evidence: Not checked online; established ACR/Arthritis Foundation principles.

osteomyelitis.name: Osteomyelitis
osteomyelitis.scope: Vertebral osteomyelitis and discitis, hematogenous seeding (S. aureus, IV drug use), contiguous spread (diabetic foot ulcer), probe-to-bone test, MRI, bone biopsy and culture, parenteral antibiotics
osteomyelitis.core: Persistent focal bone or back pain, especially with bacteremia, a deep diabetic ulcer, or elevated inflammatory markers, suggests bone infection.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Hematogenous seeding: S. aureus, endocarditis, injection drug use; vertebral disease often lacks fever
Contiguous spread: diabetic foot ulcers, pressure injury; direct inoculation: open fracture, surgery, hardware
Sickle cell: Salmonella association, but S. aureus remains important; plantar puncture through shoe → Pseudomonas

rows.label: Clues
items: Point tenderness, swelling, drainage or nonhealing sinus; systemic toxicity may be absent
★ New neurologic deficit, saddle anesthesia, urinary retention → **epidural extension/cord compression**
Diabetic ulcer over bony prominence, visible bone, or prolonged failure to heal increases suspicion
Child: fever, point tenderness over long-bone **metaphysis**; septic joint instead limits joint motion

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Infected bone develops inflammatory pressure, vascular compromise, and necrosis
Sequestrum: devitalized infected bone; involucrum: reactive new bone; biofilm promotes hardware persistence

rows.label: Dx
items: CBC, ESR/CRP, two blood-culture sets; plain films first but early findings can be absent
★ Diabetic foot: **probe-to-bone** plus radiographs/inflammatory markers; MRI if diagnosis remains uncertain
★ **MRI** best for early marrow disease and epidural/paraspinal abscess; bone scan uptake if MRI unavailable
Bone biopsy for histology/culture before antibiotics if stable; superficial wound swabs unreliable
Compatible vertebral MRI plus S. aureus bacteremia usually obviates biopsy; assess endocarditis source

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Sepsis or neurologic compromise → cultures then **IV vancomycin + cefepime**, urgent surgical assessment
Stable vertebral disease → obtain microbiologic diagnosis before empiric antibiotics
MSSA → cefazolin/nafcillin; MRSA → vancomycin; tailor to cultures, usually about **6 weeks**
IV initially for serious disease; selected stable patients can complete highly bioavailable oral regimens
Debride necrotic bone/drain abscess; surgery for instability, progressive deficit, or uncontrolled infection

rows.label: Complications
items: Epidural abscess, pathologic fracture, deformity, bacteremia, chronic draining sinus
Longstanding sinus may develop squamous carcinoma; prolonged antibiotics → line infection, renal injury, C. difficile

rows.label: Prevention
items: Diabetic foot inspection, offloading, vascular assessment, glucose control; prompt open-fracture antibiotics and debridement

rows.label: Mimics
items: Charcot arthropathy: neuropathic warm foot, joint fragmentation; MRI/biopsy may distinguish overlapping infection
Bone malignancy: destructive mass, pathology without infection
Degenerative disc disease: mechanical pain without infectious endplate/disc pattern

ovarian-cancer.name: Ovarian cancer
ovarian-cancer.scope: Epithelial ovarian carcinoma, CA-125, pelvic ultrasound, peritoneal carcinomatosis, germ cell tumors, sex cord-stromal tumors, surgical staging and cytoreduction, platinum-based chemotherapy
ovarian-cancer.core: Persistent bloating, early satiety, pelvic symptoms, or an adnexal mass—especially after menopause—requires evaluation for an often late-presenting malignancy.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Increasing age, nulliparity, BRCA1/2 or Lynch syndrome; family history of breast/ovarian cancer
Endometriosis associated with clear-cell/endometrioid subtypes; pregnancy and combined contraceptives reduce epithelial risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Older patient + ascites, large/fixed pelvic mass, weight loss, pleural effusion, obstruction → **epithelial** carcinoma
Young patient with rapidly enlarging mass → germ cell tumor; estrogen/androgen effects → stromal tumor
Postmenopausal bleeding with adnexal mass → consider estrogen-secreting granulosa tumor and endometrial disease
★ **Palpable ovary after menopause** → abnormal (ovaries atrophy); pelvic ultrasound

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Many high-grade serous tumors arise in distal fallopian tube epithelium
Transcoelomic seeding produces peritoneal/omental disease; hormone secretion depends on tumor lineage

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Transvaginal ultrasound** first; solid components, papillary projections, vascularity, ascites increase suspicion
★ **CA-125** supports risk assessment/monitoring, not diagnosis or average-risk screening
Young/complex mass → β-hCG, AFP, LDH; suspected stromal tumor → inhibin/sex hormones
Suspected malignancy → CT abdomen/pelvis/chest and gynecologic oncology; definitive histology and staging usually surgical
Isolated resectable mass → avoid aspiration; advanced disease → biopsy before neoadjuvant chemotherapy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Epithelial carcinoma → **surgical staging/cytoreduction + carboplatin/paclitaxel** according to stage
Poor upfront surgical candidate → tissue confirmation, neoadjuvant platinum chemotherapy, interval cytoreduction
Germ cell malignancy → fertility-sparing surgery when feasible; stage IA dysgerminoma may avoid chemotherapy
Higher-risk germ cell tumors → bleomycin/etoposide/cisplatin
Selected BRCA/HRD-associated disease → PARP-inhibitor maintenance after platinum response

rows.label: Complications
items: Peritoneal carcinomatosis, ascites, malignant obstruction, VTE; chemotherapy neuropathy/myelosuppression

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **No routine CA-125/ultrasound screening** in asymptomatic average-risk patients
Genetic counseling/testing; hereditary high-risk patients → discuss risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy after childbearing

rows.label: Mimics
items: Endometrioma: cyclic pain, ground-glass ultrasound; CA-125 can rise
Meigs syndrome: benign ovarian fibroma plus ascites/pleural effusion; no peritoneal implants

table.title: Tumor markers
rows: Often bilateral; psammoma bodies; WT1+, p53 abnormal

palliative-and-hospice-care.name: Palliative and hospice care
palliative-and-hospice-care.scope: Hospice eligibility, pain control, goals of care, surrogate requests
palliative-and-hospice-care.core: Palliative care relieves suffering at any illness stage; hospice centers care on comfort when prognosis and patient goals support a terminal-care benefit.

rows.label: Principle
items: ★ **Patient goals and informed consent** guide intervention burdens; symptom relief remains an obligation
Proportionate opioids for pain/dyspnea permissible despite risks; reassess sedation/respiration
Codeine fails → morphine/oxycodone; pain mimics depression; wears off early → shorten interval

rows.label: Do
items: ★ Ask understanding/values → discuss prognosis → recommend a goal-concordant plan
Assess capacity; use advance directive, then authorized surrogate: substituted judgment/best interests
★ Titrate **opioids**, short-acting for breakthrough; constipation → keep dose, add stimulant laxative

rows.label: Don't
items: DNR ≠ no antibiotics, fluids, nutrition or other desired treatment
Capable patient’s informed wishes override surrogate requests
No nonbeneficial interventions; explain reasoning, offer alternatives, seek ethics review for conflict

rows.label: Exceptions
items: Refractory terminal suffering → proportional palliative sedation, specialist review and consent
Emergency, unknown preferences → stabilize while clarifying wishes; honor documented refusals
Advanced dementia refusing intake → comfort hand-feeding by mouth; no tubes or IV

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ Hospice: **≤6-month prognosis** if usual course; longer survival permits recertification
Hospice: unrelated conditions remain treatable; no DNR requirement; enrollment revocable if goals change
Cancer pain: escalating requests → tolerance/progression, not addiction; past OUD never limits analgesia

palliative-and-hospice-care.evidence: Eligibility checked 2026-10-30: [CMS hospice benefit](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/payment/fee-for-service-providers/hospice); clinical ethics: established teaching.

table.title: Care settings
rows: Adjust with hospice team; avoid readmission

pancreatitis.name: Pancreatitis
pancreatitis.scope: Acute pancreatitis, chronic pancreatitis, exocrine and endocrine insufficiency
pancreatitis.core: Epigastric pain radiating to the back with pancreatic inflammation may be acute; repeated injury produces irreversible chronic insufficiency.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Gallstones (prior postprandial biliary colic), heavy alcohol, triglycerides >1,000 mg/dL, ERCP, hypercalcemia, medications
Chronic: prolonged alcohol/tobacco exposure, genetic disease, duct obstruction, autoimmune disease
Blunt abdominal trauma + epigastric mass/raised enzymes → contrast CT for pancreatic/duodenal injury

rows.label: Clues
items: Severe constant pain, vomiting, tenderness, ileus; chronic disease adds steatorrhea and weight loss
★ **Hypoxemia, hypotension, oliguria, persistent SIRS** → early monitored/ICU assessment

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Premature intrapancreatic enzyme activation → autodigestion and systemic inflammation
Chronic fibrosis destroys acinar/islet tissue: ↓insulin, ↓glucagon, normal insulin sensitivity; lipase may normalize

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Acute diagnosis: **2 of 3**—typical pain, lipase or amylase ≥3× ULN, characteristic imaging
RUQ ultrasound evaluates gallstones; triglycerides, calcium, liver tests identify cause
Contrast CT: diagnostic doubt, high fever/marked leukocytosis (necrosis?), deterioration, no improvement by 48–72 hours; not routine early
Chronic: CT/MRCP shows calcification/duct changes; fecal elastase <200 supports exocrine insufficiency
Recurrent, no gallstones/alcohol → EUS or MRCP for ductal anatomy; older exam questions may expect ERCP

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute: **moderate lactated Ringer resuscitation**, reassessment, IV opioid analgesia, electrolyte correction; avoid overload
★ **Early oral low-fat feeding** by 48 hours if tolerated; else enteral; older exam questions may expect initial bowel rest
Biliary with cholangitis → urgent ERCP; mild gallstone disease → cholecystectomy before discharge
Uncomplicated/sterile: no antibiotics; infected necrosis: penetrating antibiotics, delayed step-up drainage/debridement
Chronic: stop alcohol/tobacco; pancrelipase, fat-soluble vitamins, pain control; islet-loss diabetes → **insulin**, not sulfonylureas

rows.label: Complications
items: ARDS, AKI, shock, hypocalcemia; necrosis, hemorrhage; **splenic vein thrombosis** → isolated gastric varices, normal liver
Pseudocyst after >4 weeks; infected collection, obstruction; chronic disease → pancreatic cancer and brittle diabetes

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Treat cause**: gallbladder removal, triglyceride control, avoid culprit drug and alcohol
Post-ERCP rectal indomethacin in eligible patients; selected pancreatic duct stenting

rows.label: Mimics
items: Perforated ulcer: rigid abdomen/free air
Mesenteric ischemia: pain-exam mismatch; MI: ischemic ECG/troponin pattern

table.title: Severity and collections
rows: Transient dysfunction ≤48 hours or local complication

panic-disorder.name: Panic disorder
panic-disorder.scope: Panic attack criteria, unexpected recurrent attacks, agoraphobia, acute abortive therapy, maintenance therapy, medical rule-outs
panic-disorder.core: Recurrent unexpected panic attacks followed by at least 1 month of fear of recurrence or maladaptive behavioral change establish panic disorder.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Young adulthood, family history, trauma, anxiety sensitivity
Caffeine, stimulants, cannabis, decongestants, hyperthyroidism, withdrawal can provoke paniclike symptoms

rows.label: Clues
items: Abrupt intense fear peaks within minutes; palpitations, dyspnea, chest pain, paresthesias, derealization
Attack requires ≥4 characteristic symptoms; fear of dying/losing control common
★ **Syncope, exertional onset, hypoxemia, focal findings**, sustained arrhythmia → medical cause until evaluated
Agoraphobia: fear/avoidance of ≥2 situations where escape/help seems difficult, persisting ≥6 months

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Threat-circuit overactivation and catastrophic interpretation of benign sensations amplify autonomic symptoms
Hyperventilation lowers CO₂ → lightheadedness, perioral/distal tingling; avoidance reinforces anticipatory fear
**Sodium lactate infusion** provokes attacks: heightened panic sensitivity

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis after medical/substance review**; unexpected episodes distinguish disorder from predictable triggers
Vital signs, examination, ECG for cardiopulmonary symptoms; glucose/TSH or toxicology guided by history
Chest pain risk → ACS/PE evaluation rather than automatic psychiatric attribution
Assess depression, suicidality, substance use; agoraphobia may be diagnosed separately

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ During attack → **calm reassurance, slow breathing**, reduce stimulation after excluding danger
Severe acute episode → short-term lorazepam when needed; avoid with sedatives or substance-use risk
★ Maintenance → **CBT with interoceptive exposure and/or SSRI**, such as sertraline
Start SSRI low, titrate slowly; benefit takes weeks; venlafaxine alternative
Continue effective treatment after remission, then gradual taper; benzodiazepines not preferred long-term

rows.label: Complications
items: Agoraphobic avoidance, impaired function, depression, self-medication with alcohol
Benzodiazepine dependence/withdrawal; alprazolam → **between-dose rebound anxiety**; SSRIs may initially increase anxiety

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Reduce caffeine/stimulants**, regular sleep/exercise, practice exposure and relapse-prevention skills
Paper-bag rebreathing discouraged (hypoxemia risk); older exam questions may expect it if SpO₂ normal

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hyperthyroidism: persistent tremor, heat intolerance, low TSH
SVT: documented abrupt regular tachycardia, not solely subjective palpitations
Social anxiety: fear tied to scrutiny rather than unexpected attacks
Mitral valve prolapse: incidental click/murmur; doesn't explain recurrent attacks with fear of recurrence

panic-disorder.evidence: Not checked online; established DSM-5-TR and anxiety treatment teaching.

parasitic-infections.name: Parasitic infections
parasitic-infections.scope: Strongyloidiasis, giardiasis, amebiasis, cryptosporidiosis, ascariasis, schistosomiasis, pinworm (enterobiasis), cysticercosis, eosinophilia workup, antiparasitic therapy
parasitic-infections.core: Exposure, organ pattern, and immune status identify the parasite; eosinophilia favors tissue-invasive helminths rather than intestinal protozoa.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Contaminated food/water, endemic travel, freshwater contact, barefoot soil exposure, household crowding
Steroids/HTLV-1 predispose to Strongyloides hyperinfection; advanced HIV predisposes to persistent cryptosporidiosis

rows.label: Clues
items: Ascariasis: transient cough/eosinophilic infiltrates during larval migration; later intestinal or biliary obstruction
Pinworm: nocturnal perianal/vulvar itch, dysuria with normal UA; household clustering
Cysticercosis: seizures or hydrocephalus; ingestion of **T. solium eggs**, not pork cysts
Cutaneous larva migrans: soil contact; pruritic **serpiginous tracks**; animal hookworm larvae → albendazole or ivermectin

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Giardia blunts microvilli → **fat/carbohydrate malabsorption**; invasive protozoa can affect liver, urinary tract, or CNS
Strongyloides autoinfection permits lifelong persistence and dissemination after immunosuppression

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Unexplained **eosinophilia** → travel/drug history, serial stool O&P, targeted Strongyloides serology
★ Steroids + eosinophilia or infiltrates → **Strongyloides hyperinfection**: **duodenal aspirate** larvae; stool O&P often misses
Diarrhea → stool antigen/PCR for protozoa; single routine O&P can miss infection
★ Pinworm → **morning tape test** before washing; stool testing insensitive
Brain MRI/CT for cysticercosis; eye examination before antiparasitics; assess lesion viability and location

rows.label: Tx
items: Rehydrate; ascariasis → albendazole; bowel obstruction → surgical evaluation before deworming
Pinworm → albendazole, mebendazole, or pyrantel; repeat after **2 weeks**, treat household simultaneously
★ Viable parenchymal cysticercosis → albendazole ± praziquantel with corticosteroids; seizures → levetiracetam
Calcified brain lesions → no antiparasitic; hydrocephalus → neurosurgical control before cysticidal treatment

rows.label: Complications
items: Strongyloides hyperinfection → gram-negative sepsis, respiratory failure; eosinophilia may disappear
Amebic liver abscess; schistosomiasis → portal hypertension or bladder squamous carcinoma

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Screen/treat Strongyloides before **immunosuppression** after endemic exposure
Safe water, sanitation, handwashing, footwear; avoid endemic freshwater and untreated swimming water
Neurocysticercosis household contacts → **stool O&P** to find egg-shedding T. solium tapeworm carrier

rows.label: Mimics
items: IBD: chronic inflammatory diarrhea after infection excluded
Drug hypersensitivity: eosinophilia linked to new medication, rash or organ injury

table.title: Exposure → diagnosis and treatment
rows: Camping; greasy stool, bloating; stool antigen
Dysentery, flask-shaped ulcers; stool PCR; abscess → serology
Soil; larva currens, larvae in stool
Ivermectin; hyperinfection requires prolonged daily treatment
Freshwater; hematuria (haematobium), portal fibrosis (mansoni/japonicum); eggs, serology
Confirmed E. histolytica without invasive disease

parkinson-disease.name: Parkinson disease
parkinson-disease.scope: Cardinal motor symptoms (resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, postural instability/pull test), nonmotor symptoms, dopamine agonists, levodopa-carbidopa, atypical parkinsonism (PSP, MSA)
parkinson-disease.core: Progressive asymmetric bradykinesia with characteristic motor signs and levodopa responsiveness suggests Parkinson disease; early atypical features prompt another diagnosis.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older age, family susceptibility, some pesticide exposures; most disease sporadic
Dopamine-blocking antipsychotics/metoclopramide cause secondary parkinsonism rather than idiopathic disease
MPTP (synthetic heroin contaminant) → rapid parkinsonism from nigral dopaminergic neuron destruction

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Resting pill-rolling tremor, cogwheel rigidity**, reduced arm swing, shuffling gait
Freezing, micrographia, hypophonia; pull test reveals impaired postural recovery, typically later
Constipation, anosmia, REM sleep behavior disorder, depression and autonomic symptoms can precede motor disease
Early severe falls, gaze palsy, marked autonomic failure or poor treatment response → atypical syndrome

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Substantia nigra dopaminergic neuron loss; α-synuclein Lewy bodies
Reduced striatal dopamine disrupts basal ganglia motor regulation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis**; bradykinesia plus resting tremor and/or rigidity
Brain MRI for atypical findings; dopamine transporter imaging if uncertain degenerative versus nondegenerative tremor
Review medications; assess cognition, orthostatic BP, gait and swallowing

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Function-limiting motor symptoms → **carbidopa/levodopa**, preferred initial dopaminergic treatment
Pramipexole/ropinirole for selected younger patients; avoid with hallucinations, impulse-control problems or age >70
Wearing-off → adjust levodopa schedule, add MAO-B/COMT inhibitor; dyskinesia → amantadine
★ Exercise, PT/speech/swallow rehab; refractory fluctuations/tremor/dyskinesias → **deep brain stimulation**, pallidotomy
Psychosis → reduce provoking drugs; pimavanserin or selected quetiapine/clozapine, avoid potent dopamine blockers

rows.label: Complications
items: Falls, aspiration, dementia; medication → hallucinations, orthostasis, motor fluctuations/dyskinesias
Dopamine agonists → gambling/hypersexuality and sleep attacks; abrupt withdrawal → severe rigidity/hyperthermia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Fall-proof home, medication adherence, aspiration-risk assessment; no established primary neuroprotective treatment

rows.label: Mimics
items: Essential tremor: action/postural tremor without decrementing bradykinesia
Drug-induced: blocker exposure, often symmetric; normal-pressure hydrocephalus: magnetic gait, urinary/cognitive symptoms

table.title: Atypical parkinsonism
rows: Severe orthostasis/urinary dysfunction, possible cerebellar signs
Dementia before or within 1 year of parkinsonism

patient-confidentiality.name: Patient confidentiality
patient-confidentiality.scope: HIPAA, exceptions to confidentiality, Tarasoff duty to protect, mandatory reporting vs law enforcement requests, substance use privacy, subpoena vs court order
patient-confidentiality.core: Protect identifiable health information unless authorized by the patient or a specific legal basis permits disclosure.

rows.label: Principle
items: HIPAA permits treatment, payment, and health care operations disclosures without authorization

rows.label: Do
items: Verify authority, document rationale, and disclose minimum necessary information when applicable

rows.label: Don't
items: ★ Police request alone → no chart release; confirm a specific lawful basis

rows.label: Exceptions
items: ★ Report suspected child abuse and designated infections under state law
★ Tarasoff: serious threat → warn target, notify police, or hospitalize as state law requires

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Court order** → specified records only; civil subpoena alone generally insufficient
★ **Part 2 SUD records**: legal use against patient requires consent or order plus subpoena
Adult with capacity controls routine disclosures to family

patient-confidentiality.evidence: Checked HHS HIPAA Privacy Rule and 42 CFR Part 2 final rule (2024).

pediatric-hip-disorders.name: Pediatric hip disorders
pediatric-hip-disorders.scope: Developmental dysplasia of the hip, Legg-Calve-Perthes disease, slipped capital femoral epiphysis, transient synovitis, pediatric limp workup
pediatric-hip-disorders.core: A child’s limp or knee pain may originate in the hip; age, weight-bearing ability, and hip rotation separate common developmental disorders.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Breech presentation, female sex, family history → developmental hip dysplasia
Obesity and adolescence → slipped capital femoral epiphysis; atypically young/thin cases suggest endocrine disease
Recent viral illness → transient synovitis; Perthes often boys aged 4–8 years

rows.label: Clues
items: Infant asymmetric abduction or leg length; older child limp, groin/thigh/knee pain
★ **Fever, toxic appearance, refusal to bear weight**, painful restricted motion → septic arthritis concern
SCFE: obligate external rotation with flexion, limited internal rotation/abduction; Perthes: gradual painless/painful limp with limited internal rotation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Dysplasia: shallow acetabulum and unstable femoral head; Perthes: femoral-head avascular necrosis
SCFE: physeal failure displaces epiphysis relative to neck; synovitis: transient sterile joint inflammation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Examine hip in unexplained knee pain**: gait, rotation, fever; limited rotation → **hip x-ray**, not knee MRI
DDH: Ortolani reduces dislocation; Barlow provokes instability; limited abduction more useful after early infancy
Risk-based DDH imaging → ultrasound around 6 weeks; radiograph after femoral ossification, usually ≥4–6 months
Suspected septic hip → CBC, ESR/CRP, cultures, ultrasound for effusion → urgent aspiration
Kocher features: fever >38.5°C, nonweight-bearing, WBC >12,000, ESR >40; support concern, never replace aspiration

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected SCFE → **immediate nonweight-bearing**, orthopedic fixation; no forceful manipulation
★ Septic joint → **urgent drainage + IV antibiotics** after cultures when feasible
Transient synovitis → rest, NSAID, close reassessment; persistent/worsening symptoms require renewed evaluation
Perthes → orthopedic containment/ROM plan; DDH treatment depends on age and stability below

rows.label: Complications
items: Untreated dysplasia → early osteoarthritis; SCFE → avascular necrosis/chondrolysis
Perthes → femoral-head deformity; missed septic arthritis → irreversible joint destruction

rows.label: Prevention
items: Newborn and infant hip examinations; avoid tight swaddling with extended adducted hips

rows.label: Mimics
items: Osteomyelitis: focal bony tenderness, MRI marrow changes
Trauma: injury history and fracture imaging

table.title: Imaging and definitive branch
rows: Sclerosis, flattening, fragmentation; decreased bone-scan uptake

pediatric-hip-disorders.evidence: Not checked online; established pediatric orthopedic assessment principles.

pericardial-disease.name: Pericardial disease
pericardial-disease.scope: Acute pericarditis, pericardial effusion, tamponade, constrictive pericarditis
pericardial-disease.core: Pericardial inflammation, fluid accumulation, or fibrosis produces distinct chest-pain and impaired-filling syndromes; hemodynamic effect depends on accumulation rate.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Viral/idiopathic, autoimmune disease, uremia, malignancy, TB, radiation, cardiac surgery
Early post-MI inflammation or delayed immune-mediated Dressler syndrome; trauma/anticoagulation can cause hemopericardium

rows.label: Clues
items: Pericarditis: sharp pleuritic positional pain, better leaning forward; friction rub may be transient
★ Tamponade: **hypotension, elevated JVP, muffled sounds**, pulsus paradoxus >10 mmHg; triad often incomplete
Constrictive disease: edema/ascites, Kussmaul sign, pericardial knock, prominent y descent

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Inflamed surfaces cause pain; fluid or scar limits diastolic filling and stroke volume
Tamponade equalizes diastolic pressures; constriction exaggerates ventricular interdependence with respiration

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Pericarditis: ≥2 of **typical pain, rub, diffuse ST elevation/PR depression, new effusion**
Troponin elevation suggests myocardial involvement; CRP supports inflammation; echo assesses fluid and ventricular function
★ **Urgent bedside echo** for suspected tamponade: right-sided chamber collapse, plethoric IVC
Constrictive suspicion → echo, CT/MRI for thickening/calcification; catheterization if diagnosis remains uncertain

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Tamponade → **urgent pericardiocentesis**; IV fluids bridge; avoid diuresis/positive-pressure ventilation
Purulent, traumatic, malignant, or recurrent effusion → surgical drainage/window; antibiotics for bacterial cause
Stable effusion → treat cause, serial echo; low voltage alone never determines drainage
High-risk features → admit: fever, large effusion, immunosuppression, anticoagulation, subacute onset, NSAID failure
Early post-cardiac-surgery tamponade → **urgent mediastinal re-exploration**

rows.label: Complications
items: Recurrent inflammation, arrhythmia/myocarditis, obstructive shock; procedural drainage → cardiac injury
Rapid decompression can rarely cause ventricular dysfunction; NSAIDs → GI/renal injury, colchicine → diarrhea

rows.label: Prevention
items: Colchicine course: first episode 3 months; recurrence ≥6 months; taper anti-inflammatory drugs after remission
Exercise restriction until clinical/inflammatory resolution; optimize dialysis for uremic disease

rows.label: Mimics
items: STEMI: regional ST elevation with reciprocal changes; urgent coronary evaluation if uncertain
Restrictive cardiomyopathy: myocardial disease, less respiratory ventricular discordance
PE: thrombotic risk, acute RV strain

table.title: Nonemergency definitive management
rows: Ibuprofen + colchicine; aspirin preferred after MI
Selected low-dose glucocorticoid or IL-1 blockade

peripheral-artery-disease.name: Peripheral artery disease
peripheral-artery-disease.scope: Claudication, aortoiliac (Leriche) disease, critical and acute limb ischemia
peripheral-artery-disease.core: Atherosclerotic limb hypoperfusion ranges from exertional claudication to rest pain, tissue loss, or abrupt limb-threatening arterial occlusion.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Smoking, diabetes, age, CKD, hypertension, dyslipidemia; coronary/cerebrovascular atherosclerosis commonly coexists
AF, aneurysm, graft disease, hypercoagulability predispose acute occlusion

rows.label: Clues
items: Diminished pulses, cool shiny skin, hair loss, dependent rubor, distal nonhealing ulcers
★ **Pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis, poikilothermia** → acute limb ischemia
Sensory/motor deficits signal threatened limb; do not await all six findings
Abrupt onset + AF, even with prior claudication → **embolus**, not in situ thrombosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Fixed arterial narrowing limits exercise perfusion; progressive failure reduces resting tissue oxygenation
Acute embolus/thrombus prevents collateral compensation, rapidly injuring nerves and muscle
Subclavian stenosis proximal to vertebral origin → arm exercise reverses ipsilateral vertebral flow; brachiocephalic lesion: right arm + carotid

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **ABI ≤0.90** confirms PAD; 0.91–0.99 borderline; >1.40 suggests noncompressible arteries
Exertional symptoms with normal resting ABI → exercise ABI; noncompressible vessels → toe-brachial index
Duplex, CTA/MRA define anatomy when revascularization planned; acute ischemia: bedside Doppler, **arteriography with runoff**
Subclavian steal → **compare BP in both arms** (gap >15 mm Hg); confirm with duplex or **MR angiography**

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptomatic PAD: **clopidogrel or aspirin + high-intensity statin**, smoking cessation, structured exercise
Cilostazol improves claudication; contraindicated in any heart failure
Refractory disabling claudication → revascularization; chronic limb-threatening ischemia with distal target → **surgical bypass** before amputation
★ Acute ischemia → **IV unfractionated heparin, vascular consultation** without awaiting imaging; salvageable limb → urgent reperfusion
Low bleeding risk, symptomatic/postrevascularization → low-dose rivaroxaban + aspirin; no full anticoagulation solely for PAD

rows.label: Complications
items: Gangrene, infection, amputation; MI/stroke often dominate long-term mortality
Reperfusion → compartment syndrome, hyperkalemia, rhabdomyolysis; irreversible or nonfunctional limb (nonambulatory, contractures) → primary amputation
Popliteal aneurysm: pulsatile popliteal mass, distal emboli; large → **tibial nerve compression** (posterior knee/calf pain)

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Daily foot inspection**, protective footwear, diabetic foot care, BP/glucose control
Avoid thermal injury to insensate feet; antithrombotic plan after procedures based on bleeding risk

rows.label: Mimics
items: Spinal stenosis: flexion relieves walking pain, pulses preserved
Venous ulcer: medial ankle, edema, pulses intact; neuropathy: sensory loss without ischemic pulse findings
Thoracic outlet syndrome: symptoms on arm abduction, no posterior-circulation ischemia

table.title: Clinical patterns
rows: Reproducible exercise pain relieved by rest
Buttock claudication, erectile dysfunction, weak femorals
Calf claudication; normal femoral, weak pedal pulses
Arm-exercise dizziness/syncope or claudication; weak ipsilateral pulse

peripheral-neuropathy.name: Peripheral neuropathy
peripheral-neuropathy.scope: Distal symmetric polyneuropathy, chemotherapy-induced (cisplatin, paclitaxel), HIV-associated neuropathy, alcohol-related, neuropathic pain pharmacotherapy (TCAs, gabapentinoids, SNRIs)
peripheral-neuropathy.core: Length-dependent injury produces symmetric distal sensory symptoms beginning in the feet and progressing proximally before the hands become involved.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Diabetes, alcohol use, CKD, B12 deficiency, monoclonal gammopathy, HIV
Cisplatin/paclitaxel exposure; older neurotoxic ART such as stavudine; malnutrition

rows.label: Clues
items: Burning pain, allodynia or numbness; reduced vibration, ankle reflexes and distal sensation
★ **Asymmetry, rapid progression, motor predominance or marked autonomic findings** → urgent expanded evaluation
Small-fiber neuropathy: pain/temperature loss with initially preserved strength and nerve conduction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Axonal dying-back affects longest fibers first; demyelinating neuropathy produces disproportionate conduction slowing

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Glucose/A1c, B12 with methylmalonic acid if borderline, SPEP with immunofixation**
CBC, metabolic panel, TSH; HIV testing according to exposure and clinical context
EMG/nerve conduction for atypical features, unclear diagnosis, or suspected demyelination
Normal studies do not exclude small-fiber disease; skin biopsy can confirm selected cases

rows.label: Tx
items: Treat cause: glycemic control, B12, alcohol cessation/nutrition, optimize ART; review neurotoxic drugs
★ Pain → **duloxetine, gabapentin/pregabalin, or TCA**; choose by comorbidity and adverse effects
Gabapentinoids: sedation/edema, renal dose adjustment; TCAs: anticholinergic effects, cardiac risk in older adults
★ Painful chemotherapy neuropathy → **duloxetine**; discuss dose reduction/substitution with oncology
Topical lidocaine/capsaicin for localized symptoms; avoid chronic opioids

rows.label: Complications
items: Falls, painless ulcers, infection, Charcot arthropathy; orthostatic hypotension with autonomic involvement
Pain treatment reduces symptoms without restoring lost sensation

rows.label: Prevention
items: Daily foot inspection, protective footwear, monofilament assessment, fall prevention
Treat nutritional deficiencies; monitor symptoms during neurotoxic chemotherapy

rows.label: Mimics
items: Radiculopathy: dermatomal, often asymmetric pain and weakness
Myelopathy: hyperreflexia, sensory level, bowel/bladder dysfunction
Peripheral arterial disease: exertional pain, reduced pulses rather than sensory stocking loss
Charcot-Marie-Tooth: adolescent **pes cavus, hammer toes**, distal wasting, slowed conduction, family history

pharyngitis.name: Pharyngitis
pharyngitis.scope: Centor score, Group A Streptococcus, rapid antigen detection, throat culture, viral pharyngitis, penicillin, peritonsillar abscess
pharyngitis.core: Most sore throats are viral; identify patients needing group A streptococcal testing and recognize deep-space infection or airway danger.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: School-age children, close contacts, crowded settings, winter/spring; GAS uncommon below age 3
Smoking, immunosuppression, incomplete vaccination broaden infectious differential

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Cough, rhinorrhea, conjunctivitis, oral ulcers** favor viral cause; avoid unnecessary GAS testing
Centor: fever, tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical nodes, absence of cough; 1 point each
McIsaac modifies by age; score 0–1 → no test, no antibiotic; scoring never proves bacterial infection
★ **Trismus, muffled voice, unilateral bulge, uvular deviation** → peritonsillar abscess

rows.label: Pathophys
items: GAS pharyngeal infection can trigger immune-mediated rheumatic fever or glomerulonephritis
Tonsillitis → peritonsillar pus: **GAS** commonest, often mixed anaerobes; deeper spread threatens airway, vessels

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ No clear viral syndrome and elevated clinical score → **rapid antigen test or NAAT**
Negative rapid antigen in symptomatic child ≥3 → throat culture; adults usually need no backup
Positive test with compatible illness → treat; asymptomatic carriage generally needs no eradication
Abscess usually clinical; ultrasound/contrast neck CT if uncertain or deep-space extension suspected

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Confirmed GAS → **penicillin or amoxicillin for 10 days**; IM benzathine penicillin if adherence uncertain
Penicillin allergy: cephalexin if nonimmediate; azithromycin/clindamycin if immediate, accounting for local resistance
Viral illness → fluids, warm saline gargle, acetaminophen/ibuprofen; no antibiotics
★ Peritonsillar abscess → **drainage + amoxicillin-clavulanate**; airway assessment, IV ampicillin-sulbactam if severe

rows.label: Complications
items: Rheumatic fever prevented by timely GAS antibiotics; poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis not reliably prevented
Retropharyngeal spread, airway obstruction; Fusobacterium → internal jugular thrombophlebitis/Lemierre syndrome

rows.label: Prevention
items: Hand hygiene; remain home until afebrile and ≥12–24 hours after effective GAS antibiotics
Do not routinely test asymptomatic household contacts or obtain test-of-cure

rows.label: Mimics
items: EBV: posterior nodes, splenomegaly, amoxicillin-associated rash
Epiglottitis: drooling, tripod posture, stridor; avoid provocative throat examination
Diphtheria: adherent gray membrane, incomplete vaccination

phobias.name: Phobias
phobias.scope: Specific phobia (flying, heights, blood-injection-injury), exposure therapy, situational benzodiazepines, social anxiety disorder (generalized vs performance-only), beta-blockers, agoraphobia
phobias.core: Persistent disproportionate fear leads to avoidance or endurance with intense distress, producing impairment despite recognition that danger is limited.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Temperamental inhibition, family anxiety, frightening experiences or learned fear; often childhood/adolescent onset

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Fear reliably provoked by trigger; duration **≥6 months**, excessive relative to actual/cultural danger
Anticipatory anxiety and avoidance limit school, work, medical care or travel
Blood-injection-injury subtype may produce vasovagal syncope rather than persistent tachycardia

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Conditioned threat response and avoidance prevent extinction; relief from escape reinforces fear

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical assessment** of trigger, feared consequence, avoidance and impairment
Agoraphobia: fear in ≥2 categories—transport, open/enclosed spaces, crowds/lines, outside home alone
Exclude substances, hyperthyroidism, arrhythmia or pulmonary disease when bodily symptoms atypical
Symptoms only with feared trigger, normal exam → psychiatric evaluation, not pheochromocytoma/Holter workup

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Graded exposure-based CBT** first-line across phobic disorders
Blood-injection-injury: applied muscle tension during exposure reduces fainting
Generalized social anxiety: CBT or sertraline/escitalopram; venlafaxine alternative
★ Performance-only social anxiety → situational **propranolol**; asthma/bradycardia → short-acting benzodiazepine instead
Rare trigger (flight, MRI) → short-acting benzodiazepine (**↑GABA-A**); routine use risks dependence, impairs exposure

rows.label: Complications
items: Social/occupational restriction, depression, substance misuse; avoidance of necessary health care
Beta-blocker hypotension; benzodiazepine sedation, falls, impaired driving

rows.label: Prevention
items: Early treatment, repeated graduated practice and reduced avoidance help maintain gains
Avoid self-medication with alcohol; include relapse-prevention exposure plans

rows.label: Mimics
items: Panic disorder: recurrent unexpected attacks; fear of further attacks
OCD: intrusive obsessions and rituals drive avoidance
Avoidant personality: pervasive longstanding inadequacy/rejection sensitivity, often coexists with social anxiety

phobias.evidence: Social anxiety care checked 2026-10-30: [NIMH](https://www.nimh.nih.gov/health/publications/social-anxiety-disorder-more-than-just-shyness); established exposure-based care.

physician-patient-communication.name: Physician-patient communication
physician-patient-communication.scope: Medical interpreters, limited English proficiency, delivering bad news, empathetic communication, family requests to withhold information
physician-patient-communication.core: Respect autonomy through understandable, honest, empathic dialogue; identify what patients understand and want before sharing decisions or sensitive information.

rows.label: Principle
items: Confidentiality, cultural humility, informed choice; language barriers never imply impaired capacity
Patient preferences determine family involvement and desired level of disclosure
**Comprehensive, contextual care**: whole-person, longitudinal; tailored to culture, family, goals

rows.label: Do
items: ★ **Qualified medical interpreter**, free to patient; speak directly to patient in short segments
★ Bad news: privacy → understanding/preferences → warning → plain disclosure → empathy → plan
Validate emotion; open questions, silence, teach-back; explore beliefs before correcting misinformation

rows.label: Don't
items: Avoid jargon, false reassurance, interrupting, arguing, blaming, or premature advice
Avoid routine reliance on children/family for interpreting consent or sensitive discussions
Avoid promising cure or confidentiality beyond legal limits

rows.label: Exceptions
items: ★ **Family requests nondisclosure → ask patient privately**; patient preferences control disclosure
